verified_ref: Maha Upanishad (Mahopanishad) ch. 6, within the block numbered 6.66-82 in T. R. Srinivasa Ayyangar's Adyar translation (1941); exact verse number 6.68 not independently confirmed (the Sanskrit text on sanskritdocuments.org is behind a bot challenge).
attribution_note: Chapters 3-6 of the Maha Upanishad are Ribhu's teaching to his son/disciple Nidagha, and chapter 6 addresses Nidagha by name, so Ribhu -> Nidagha is right.
translation_note: Fair. The Adyar rendering (following Upanishad-brahma-yogin) frames it as how a liberated person should 'wander the earth': showing busyness outwardly while free of agitation at heart, seemingly a doer but without the urge to act. 'Kartā bahir akartāntaḥ' literally 'doer outside, non-doer inside'; our 'unhurried inside' in the line softens 'free of agitation' but is acceptable.
context: In the last chapter of the Maha Upanishad, Ribhu describes the jivanmukta, someone free while still living. Just before, he says such a person does each day's tasks as they come, treats friend and foe alike and speaks pleasantly. This verse belongs to a run of refrains telling Nidagha to 'move through the world' in that way; it is followed by the 'this one is mine, that one is not' verse.

key_terms.sense: outward zeal or bustle that is put on to suit the occasion
free of agitation in the heart
a doer outside, a non-doer within
move about, live and roam in the world

core_teaching: A free person can be fully engaged in worldly work while the inner self stays untouched by its excitement and anxiety. Action is not abandoned; only the inner identification with being the anxious doer is dropped.

commentaries.who: Upanishad-brahma-yogin (Advaita), as rendered in T. R. Srinivasa Ayyangar's Adyar translation (1941)
commentaries.gist: The liberated sage keeps a show of interest in worldly affairs, like a temple-tower figurine that only seems to hold the tower up, while the heart stays still; like a skilled actor, partly to set an example.

practical_reading: Teachers use it for people in demanding jobs or caregiving: give the task your full energy and visible effort, but don't let the urgency take over your inner life. The busyness is real; the panic is optional.
misreadings: Not a licence to be fake or manipulative with people
Not advice to suppress feelings; it describes inner freedom, not emotional numbness
Not a call to withdraw from work
cautions: The commentary's 'actor' image can sound like pretending; present it as role-playing without being swallowed by the role
Someone burned out may hear 'stay calm inside' as another demand; pair it with rest, not more effort
speaks_to: people in high-pressure roles (doctors, managers, parents of young children)
wanting to stay engaged without losing oneself
not_for: someone in acute burnout who needs permission to stop
grief, where 'calm inside' can feel like being told not to feel
research_note: Only one commentary source found (the Maha Upanishad has no classical bhashya besides Upanishad-brahma-yogin). Ayyangar's 1941 translation may still be in copyright; paraphrased only. Many Maha Upanishad verses in chapters 5-6 also occur in the Yoga Vasishtha; I could not locate this particular verse in the Pansikar Yoga Vasishtha text I searched.

verified_ref: Maha Upanishad ch. 6, same block (6.66-82 in the Adyar translation); widely cited as Maha Upanishad 6.71-72. The first half of the verse also stands in the Yoga Vasishtha, Upashama Prakarana 5.18.61 (Pansikar ed.), with a different second half.
attribution_note: Ribhu to Nidagha, Maha Upanishad ch. 6. Note the parallel: in the Yoga Vasishtha the same first line is spoken by Vasishtha to Rama.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Bandhu' is kinsman/relative ('this one is our relative, that one is not'); 'laghu-cetasām' = of the small-minded; 'udāra-caritānām' = of those of noble or generous conduct. Our translation and line are fine.
context: Still describing how the liberated person lives, Ribhu contrasts narrow and generous minds. Just before, Nidagha is told to act in the world like a skilled actor, inwardly detached. In the Upanishad's own frame (per the Adyar commentary) the verse leads into identifying with the cosmic self (Virat), so that all beings are one's own family; then comes the teaching that bondage is the mind's pull toward objects.

key_terms.sense: 'this one is a relative (one of mine), this one is not'
of those whose conduct is generous, noble

core_teaching: Dividing people into 'mine' and 'not mine' is a mark of a small mind; a large-hearted person treats everyone as family. In the Upanishad this flows from seeing one self in all, not merely from social niceness.

commentaries.who: Upanishad-brahma-yogin (Advaita), as rendered by T. R. Srinivasa Ayyangar (Adyar, 1941)
commentaries.gist: Reads 'the earth' as the world of the cosmic self (Virat); the large-hearted treat it as their family, and Ribhu urges Nidagha to identify with that cosmic self and so leave behind birth, ageing and death.

commentaries.who: Yoga Vasishtha 5.18.61 with the Tatparya-prakasha commentary (Pansikar ed., Sanskrit)
commentaries.gist: Same first line; the second half says the noble have an unveiled mind, which the commentary explains as a mind free of the narrowing 'only this one is my kin', seeing sameness everywhere.

practical_reading: Used today as an ethic of inclusion: notice when you sort people into 'ours' and 'theirs' (family, caste, nation, team) and widen the circle of care. Teachers also apply it to everyday generosity toward strangers and colleagues.
misreadings: Not a political slogan about borders or a claim that all differences are unreal in practical life
Not a demand to treat strangers exactly as one's own children or to neglect one's own family
The verse itself is about inner largeness, not about a world government
cautions: Extremely well known and often quoted out of context; keep its Upanishadic frame (seeing one self in all)
Someone hurt by family may find 'everyone is family' painful; family here is a circle of goodwill, not obligation to an abuser
speaks_to: workplace or community conflict between groups
migrants and people far from home
not_for: someone estranged from an abusive family
use as a rebuke to a person setting healthy boundaries
research_note: Exact verse number in the Maha Upanishad not independently confirmed (sanskritdocuments.org blocked by bot challenge); 6.71-72 is the common citation. The Yoga Vasishtha parallel was checked in the Sanskrit OCR of the Pansikar edition.

verified_ref: Maitri (Maitrayaniya) Upanishad 1.4 in Max Müller's numbering (SBE 15, 1884, 'Maitrayana-brahmana Upanishad' I.4); within paragraphs 2-7 of Prapathaka I in the Adyar 108-Upanishad recension.
attribution_note: Spoken by King Brihadratha of the Ikshvaku line to the sage Shakayanya (Müller: 'the Saint Sakayanya'). Correct.
translation_note: Accurate. Our Sanskrit is only the opening clause of a long sentence: Brihadratha goes on to list great kings, demigods, oceans, mountains and even the pole star as passing away. Both Müller and the Adyar translation say 'perish like grass' or 'herbs and trees, growing and decaying'.
context: Brihadratha has handed his kingdom to his son and gone to the forest for long austerity. When the sage Shakayanya appears and offers a boon, the king asks to be taught the self. Shakayanya first tries to put him off, and the king answers with this lament on the decay of the body and of everything in the world. It builds to the 'frog in a well' plea for help.

key_terms.sense: springing up only to be destroyed

core_teaching: Everything we see, from insects to kings to the stars, comes into being and falls apart. The king's lament is the turning point that makes him ready to ask what does not perish.

commentaries.who: Max Müller tr., SBE 15 (1884), with notes drawing on Ramatirtha's commentary
commentaries.gist: Places the line in the king's verse lament (gatha) on the body's impurity and the world's decay; notes manuscript variants in the grass/trees compound and in the list of departed kings, which even the commentator calls corrupt.

commentaries.who: Upanishad-brahma-yogin (Advaita), as rendered by T. R. Srinivasa Ayyangar (Adyar, 1941)
commentaries.gist: Frames the speech as a verse disparaging worldly existence: whatever is mortal is perishable like flies and gnats that perish as quickly as grass, so pursuing desires in such a body is pointless.

practical_reading: Teachers use the king's survey of impermanence as an honest starting point: noticing that things pass is not pessimism but the beginning of asking what really matters. It can help someone loosen their grip on status or possessions.
misreadings: Not a claim that life is worthless or that one should despair
Not contempt for small creatures; the image is about how briefly they last
cautions: A stark verse about everything dying; risky for a reader who is depressed, grieving or has suicidal thoughts
The wider passage describes the body in disgusting terms (bones, mucus, faeces); don't quote around it
speaks_to: after a loss of status, job or wealth
people chasing achievement who feel empty
not_for: fresh grief
depression or hopelessness
anyone in crisis

verified_ref: Maitri Upanishad 1.4 (end of the same paragraph) in Müller's SBE 15 numbering; the passage is paragraphs 2-7 of Prapathaka I in the Adyar recension, which is probably where our '1.7' comes from.
translation_note: Our ref '1.7' conflicts with the sibling verse up_maitrayani.8 at '1.4' though both are in Müller's 1.4; pick one numbering system. 'Andhodapāna' is literally a 'blind' (i.e. dry or dark) well: Müller renders 'dry well', the Adyar translation 'a reservoir of water of the form of a well'. 'Dark well' is acceptable.
context: This closes King Brihadratha's lament. After listing everything that passes away, he asks what use pleasures are if those who enjoy them keep returning to this world, and begs the sage to pull him out. In the next section Shakayanya, pleased, begins teaching him about the self.

key_terms.sense: a frog sitting in a blind (dry, dark) well
you are our way, our refuge

core_teaching: Pleasures cannot lift someone out of the round of repetition; the king sees himself trapped like a frog in a well and asks a teacher for a way out. Asking for help is the turning point.

commentaries.who: Max Müller tr., SBE 15 (1884)
commentaries.gist: Renders the image as a frog in a dry well and the plea as 'thou art my way' repeated twice; notes the commentator's reading of a disputed word in the clause about who feeds on pleasures.

commentaries.who: Upanishad-brahma-yogin (Advaita), as rendered by T. R. Srinivasa Ayyangar (Adyar, 1941)
commentaries.gist: Reads the king as already disgusted with worldly life and asking to be reclaimed; the teacher is the only resort for people of his kind who have fallen into this miserable existence.

practical_reading: Feeling stuck, as if the walls of your life are all you can see, is a reasonable moment to ask for guidance. Teachers use the frog image for the limited view we get trapped in, and the plea as a model of humbly asking for help.
misreadings: Not a statement that the person is helpless or worthless
Not a rejection of all enjoyment; it questions pleasure as the answer to the deeper problem
cautions: The 'return here again and again' refers to rebirth; may need gentle framing
Language of being trapped can resonate with depression; pair with the sage's positive response that follows
speaks_to: ready to ask for help or find a mentor
not_for: acute crisis or suicidal feelings, where 'lift me out of this world' could be misread
someone who needs practical rather than spiritual help
research_note: Numbering systems differ: Müller (and Cowell) put the whole lament in 1.2-1.4; the Adyar recension numbers its paragraphs 1.2-1.7.

verified_ref: Maitri Upanishad 6.34, verse (3) in Müller's SBE 15 (Maitrayana-brahmana Upanishad VI.34); in the shorter Adyar recension the same verses are in Prapathaka IV.3.
attribution_note: Part of Shakayanya's teaching to Brihadratha, though by 6.34 the frame has thinned: the verses are introduced as 'on this there are the following verses'. 'Shakayanya -> Brihadratha' is acceptable.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Citta' is mind/thought; Müller: thoughts alone cause the round of births, so purify them; what a man thinks, that he is. 'Tanmaya' = made of that, becomes that.
context: Near the end of the Maitri, after long passages on sacrifice and meditation, a run of eleven verses on the mind is given. Just before this one, the text says thoughts become still like a fire without fuel, and that even a truth-loving mind can be pulled by sense objects. Next it says a serene mind wipes out good and bad deeds.

key_terms.sense: the mind itself is the round of worldly existence
one should purify it with effort
what one's mind holds, that one becomes

core_teaching: Our experience of the world is shaped by the mind, and we gradually become what we dwell on. So the work is to clean up the mind with steady effort.

commentaries.who: Max Müller tr., SBE 15 (1884)
commentaries.gist: Translates it as thoughts alone causing the round of births and notes how close this is to the opening of the Dhammapada; records a manuscript reading 'samsara' in place of the commentator's text.

commentaries.who: Upanishad-brahma-yogin (Advaita), as rendered by T. R. Srinivasa Ayyangar (Adyar, 1941)
commentaries.gist: The mind alone is worldly existence because it hides Brahman; it should be uprooted by study and by seeing there is no mind apart from Brahman. Whatever one sets the mind on, one finally becomes.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to say: watch what you feed your attention (worries, grudges, screens, gratitude), because you become what you dwell on. Mental hygiene is daily work.
misreadings: Not 'think positive and everything will be fine'
Not a claim that outer problems are imaginary or that suffering is your own fault
cautions: Can sound like blaming someone's own mind for their anxiety or depression; frame as an invitation, not an accusation
Not a substitute for treatment of clinical anxiety or OCD (where 'purify your thoughts' can feed obsession)
speaks_to: anger or resentment that keeps replaying
not_for: someone with OCD or intrusive thoughts
trauma survivors who might hear 'it's all in your mind'

verified_ref: Maitri Upanishad 6.34, verse (5) in Müller's SBE 15; Prapathaka IV.3 in the Adyar recension.
translation_note: Accurate. Müller: if a man's thoughts were as fixed on Brahman as on worldly things, who would not be freed?
context: Fourth and fifth of the verses on the mind at Maitri 6.34. Just before, a serene mind is said to burn up good and bad deeds and gain lasting happiness. Just after, the text says the mind is of two kinds, pure and impure, according to whether it is touched by desire.
core_teaching: We already have a great capacity for focus; it is just spent on objects. Turned toward the highest, the same intensity would free us.

commentaries.who: Max Müller tr., SBE 15 (1884)
commentaries.gist: Renders the verse plainly as a conditional: thoughts fixed on Brahman as firmly as on worldly things would bring freedom; it sits among verses Ramatirtha's commentary treats as summary slokas.

commentaries.who: Upanishad-brahma-yogin (Advaita), as rendered by T. R. Srinivasa Ayyangar (Adyar, 1941)
commentaries.gist: Adds that bondage comes from the mind straying outward instead of facing the inner self; the same saturation the mind has with pleasures, if absorbed in Brahman, would liberate anyone.

practical_reading: Your capacity for devotion is visible in what you already obsess about; teachers suggest redirecting some of that energy toward what you most value. A gentle, encouraging verse about attention.
misreadings: Not a scolding for enjoying anything
Not a promise that liberation is quick or easy
cautions: Mild verse; few risks. Avoid implying the reader is failing spiritually.
speaks_to: distraction and phone or media habits
wanting to deepen a spiritual practice
not_for: someone already harsh on themselves about lack of discipline

verified_ref: Maitri Upanishad 6.34, verse (11) in Müller's SBE 15; Prapathaka IV.3 in the Adyar recension. Also Amritabindu (Brahmabindu) Upanishad v. 2 (Aiyar's Thirty Minor Upanishads).
attribution_note: Same frame as up_maitrayani.78. The parallel in the Amritabindu Upanishad, noted in our_note, is confirmed.
translation_note: Accurate. Müller: mind alone is the cause of bondage and liberty; attached to the world it is bound, free from the world it is liberty.
context: This is the last of the eleven verses on the mind at Maitri 6.34. It comes right after the image of water poured into water, fire into fire: a mind merged in the self can no longer be told apart and is free. The prose that follows says those who neglect the fire rites and meditation miss the place of Brahman. The same verse opens the Amritabindu Upanishad, which pairs it with the pure and impure mind.

key_terms.sense: the cause of both bondage and liberation

core_teaching: What binds or frees us is not the world itself but the mind's attachment to it. The same mind that hooks onto things can let go of them, and in letting go there is freedom.

commentaries.who: Max Müller tr., SBE 15 (1884)
commentaries.gist: Gives the verse as the last of eleven slokas on mind; notes the manuscript reading 'vishayasaktam muktyai' and the commentator's view that the preceding line is easy, which Müller disputes.

commentaries.who: Upanishad-brahma-yogin (Advaita), as rendered by T. R. Srinivasa Ayyangar (Adyar, 1941)
commentaries.gist: The mind engrossed in worldly pleasures leads to bondage; freed from their influence it leads to liberation. Explanations of liberation other than this inward turn are called mere book learning.

commentaries.who: Amritabindu Upanishad 1-2, tr. K. Narayanasvami Aiyar (1914)
commentaries.gist: The same verse follows the teaching that mind is pure or impure according to desire; the aspirant should therefore keep the mind free of longing for sense objects.

practical_reading: Freedom starts with noticing what your mind is hooked on; you cannot always change circumstances, but you can work on the grip. Teachers use it to introduce non-attachment as a skill.
misreadings: Not 'your suffering is your own fault'
Not a claim that external injustice or illness doesn't matter
'Free of objects' does not mean blank or uncaring
cautions: Can feel dismissive to someone facing real external hardship (abuse, poverty, illness)
For clinical anxiety or depression, add that skills and support matter; this is not a cure
not_for: victims of abuse or injustice, where it could sound like 'just change your attitude'
fresh grief

verified_ref: Maitreya Upanishad 2.1 (opening of chapter II; tr. K. Narayanasvami Aiyar, Thirty Minor Upanishads, 1914). The same verses recur in the Skanda Upanishad (vv. 10-12 in the Adyar numbering).
attribution_note: Correct: Maitreya goes to Kailasa and asks Mahadeva for the highest truth; Mahadeva answers with this verse.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Nirmālya' is the remains of yesterday's offerings (withered flowers) removed before fresh worship; Aiyar 'cast-off offerings'. 'So'ham bhāvena' = with the conviction 'I am He'.
context: Chapter 1 of the Maitreya Upanishad retells the Maitri story of Brihadratha. In chapter 2 the sage Maitreya goes to Kailasa and asks Shiva for the highest truth. Shiva answers by turning outer temple worship into an inner one: the body is the shrine, the living self is Shiva, and ignorance is the stale offering to clear away. The verses that follow redefine knowledge, meditation, bathing and purity, then describe the renunciant's life.

key_terms.sense: the living being is Shiva alone
ignorance as the withered offerings to be removed
worship with the sense 'I am He'

core_teaching: The truest temple is your own body and the divine is your own deepest self; real worship is dropping ignorance and recognising 'I am That'.

commentaries.who: K. Narayanasvami Aiyar tr., Maitreya Upanishad II (Thirty Minor Upanishads, 1914)
commentaries.gist: Gives the verse as Mahadeva's reply to Maitreya's request for the highest truth, followed by the renunciant's rules: begging food, contemplating non-duality, the body as impure and to be washed.

commentaries.who: Upanishad-brahma-yogin (Advaita), on the parallel verses in the Skanda Upanishad, as rendered by T. R. Srinivasa Ayyangar (Adyar, 1941)
commentaries.gist: Explains this as mental worship, the essential means to self-knowledge: the jiva is the Shiva installed in the body-temple, ignorance is thrown away like faded flowers from the altar, and worship is the conviction 'I am the deity'.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to make worship inward and daily: treat your body with respect as a shrine, and clear away what clouds your sense of the sacred in you. It also supports self-respect.
misreadings: Not 'I am God, so I can do as I please'
Not a rejection of temple worship for householders; it is addressed to renunciants
'Body is a temple' here is not a fitness slogan, though care for the body fits
cautions: The same chapter soon calls the body impure and foul, so don't pair the two passages carelessly
Strongly non-dual ('I am Shiva'); some devotional readers may find it presumptuous
not_for: someone with an eating disorder, if it slips into rules about purity
readers strongly committed to dualist devotion, without explanation
research_note: No classical commentary on the Maitreya Upanishad itself was found online; the second gist is Upanishad-brahma-yogin on the identical verses in the Skanda Upanishad.

verified_ref: Maitreya Upanishad 2.2 (Aiyar, Thirty Minor Upanishads); same verse in the Skanda Upanishad (Adyar vv. 10-12).
attribution_note: Mahadeva to Maitreya, continuing from 2.1. Correct.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Abheda-darśanam' = seeing non-difference (between oneself and the divine/others); 'nirviṣayaṃ manaḥ' = a mind withdrawn from objects. Our line 'a mind at rest' is a slight softening of 'free of objects' but acceptable.
context: Continuing his answer to Maitreya, Shiva redefines four daily religious acts in inner terms: knowledge, meditation, ritual bathing and ritual purity. The next lines tell the renunciant to drink the nectar of Brahman, beg only enough food to keep the body going, and live alone thinking of the One.

key_terms.sense: meditation is a mind free of objects
bathing is giving up the mind's impurities
purity is restraint of the senses

core_teaching: Outer rituals point to inner disciplines: real knowledge is seeing oneness, real meditation is a mind let go of objects, real bathing is washing out mental stains, real purity is mastery of the senses.

commentaries.who: K. Narayanasvami Aiyar tr., Maitreya Upanishad II (1914)
commentaries.gist: Renders the four definitions as cognition of everything as non-different from oneself, drawing the mind from sense objects, purifying the mind's impurities, and subduing the senses.

commentaries.who: Upanishad-brahma-yogin (Advaita), on the Skanda Upanishad parallel, as rendered by T. R. Srinivasa Ayyangar (1941)
commentaries.gist: Knowledge is seeing the identity of the individual and the Supreme; ablution is giving up impure mental tendencies (vasanas); purification is control of both inner and outer senses.

commentaries.who: Skanda Upanishad, tr. K. Narayanasvami Aiyar (1914)
commentaries.gist: The same four definitions appear, followed by begging for alms, living alone and dwelling on the non-dual One as the path to liberation.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to reinterpret daily routines: as you bathe, also let go of a grudge; as you clean, also rein in a habit. It helps people for whom ritual has gone mechanical.
misreadings: Not a dismissal of physical hygiene or of ritual for those who value it
'Seeing no difference' is not denial of real differences in need or justice
cautions: Addressed to renunciants; for householders frame it as an inner layer added to ordinary life, not a call to abandon it
not_for: someone with OCD around cleanliness or purity
readers who may take 'restraint of the senses' as a demand for harsh self-denial

verified_ref: Mundaka Upanishad 1.1.3 (same in all editions checked: S. Sitarama Sastri 1905 with Shankara; Vasu 1909 with Madhva).
attribution_note: Narrative verse: Shaunaka is the questioner and Angiras the teacher. Listing Shaunaka as speaker is fine.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Mahāśāla' = great householder (lit. having a great hall); Madhva's translator renders 'of the great sacrifices'. 'Vidhivad upasannaḥ' = approached duly, as the scriptures prescribe.
context: The Mundaka opens with the lineage of the teaching from Brahma down to Angiras. Then Shaunaka, a wealthy householder, comes to Angiras in the prescribed way with one question: what is it that, once known, makes everything known? Angiras answers by distinguishing two kinds of knowledge.

key_terms.sense: great householder, a man of large estate
having approached (the teacher) in the proper way

key_terms.term: kasmin vijñāte sarvam idaṃ vijñātaṃ bhavati
key_terms.sense: by knowing what does all this become known?

core_teaching: The seeker asks for the one reality behind all the variety of things, the way knowing gold lets you understand every gold ornament. Asking that question properly, with humility, is where the path starts.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. S. Sitarama Sastri (1905)
commentaries.gist: 'Duly' shows the rule for approaching a teacher applies to everyone, not only Shaunaka. The question assumes one cause of all variety, as knowing gold lets one know all the different gold pieces.

commentaries.who: Madhva school (Dvaita), tr. S. C. Vasu (1909), translator's note on Madhva's reading
commentaries.gist: Treats the question as threefold: what authoritative teaching reveals rites and deities, what more must be known to grasp their fruit, and what more is needed actually to gain it.

practical_reading: Behind many scattered worries lies one real question; teachers use Shaunaka as a model of bringing that question humbly to someone who knows. Success in worldly life (he was a rich householder) did not answer it.
misreadings: Not a promise of encyclopaedic knowledge of every fact
Not a claim that worldly learning is useless
cautions: Low risk. Mentions a formal teacher relationship; for readers without a guru, frame as seeking good guidance.
speaks_to: successful people who feel something is missing
curiosity about what life is ultimately about
not_for: someone needing immediate practical comfort in crisis

verified_ref: Mundaka Upanishad 1.1.4-5 (two verses joined; numbering same in Shankara and Madhva editions).
translation_note: Accurate. Shankara reads 'adhigamyate' as 'is reached' and says reaching here simply means knowing (the removal of ignorance). Our line's 'all our learning and skills' is a modern widening of the list of Vedic sciences; acceptable but note the original 'lower' list is the Vedas themselves.
context: Asked for the one thing that makes all known, Angiras first says there are two kinds of knowledge to be known, the higher and the lower. He lists the four Vedas and six auxiliary sciences as lower, and calls the higher that by which the imperishable is reached. The following verses describe that imperishable as the source of all beings.
core_teaching: All learning, even of scripture, is lower knowledge; the higher knowledge is the direct knowing of what never perishes. Shankara stresses this is not mastering the Upanishad's words but realising what they point to.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. S. Sitarama Sastri (1905)
commentaries.gist: Lower knowledge concerns the means and fruits of good and bad acts; higher is knowing the supreme self. Even the Upanishads as mere words are lower; the higher is the realisation they convey, needing a teacher and renunciation.

commentaries.who: Madhva (Dvaita), tr. S. C. Vasu (1909)
commentaries.gist: The same Vedas are lower when used only for ritual and higher when understood as speaking of Vishnu; there is really one body of scripture, read in two ways.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to separate information and skill from wisdom: degrees and expertise are valuable but do not by themselves settle the question of meaning. Keep learning, and also seek what learning points beyond.
misreadings: Not contempt for science, skills or education
Not a claim that the Vedas are false; Shankara keeps them as valid in their sphere
cautions: Calling all learning 'lower' can sting a student under exam pressure; frame as two complementary kinds.
speaks_to: students and professionals who feel knowledge isn't enough
not_for: someone who left education and feels inadequate, if it is read as dismissing their worth

verified_ref: Mundaka Upanishad 1.2.8 (all editions checked). Near-identical verse at Katha Upanishad 1.2.5.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Jaṅghanyamānāḥ' = battered, afflicted; Shankara: by old age, sickness and many troubles. Our 'stumbling' is a fair image.
context: Angiras has just described the Vedic sacrifices and their heavenly rewards, then called them 'unsafe boats' that cannot carry one across. This verse describes those who trust in rituals and rewards while thinking themselves wise. The next verses say such people return to lower worlds once their merit runs out, and that a true seeker turns away from works to find a teacher.

key_terms.sense: dwelling in the midst of ignorance
wise and learned in their own estimation
like the blind led by the blind

core_teaching: People who equate religious busyness or status with wisdom wander in circles of suffering, and lead others the same way. Self-satisfaction blocks learning.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. S. Sitarama Sastri (1905)
commentaries.gist: They flatter themselves that they know all that is worth knowing, and wander afflicted by old age and sickness, like blind men following a blind guide into ditches and thorns.

commentaries.who: Madhva school (Dvaita), tr. S. C. Vasu (1909)
commentaries.gist: Rendered as fools, wise in their own eyes and oppressed by misery, going round and round like the blind led by the blind; no separate bhashya note on this verse.

practical_reading: Teachers use it as a check on spiritual or intellectual arrogance and on following confident leaders blindly. Ask whether you, or the people you follow, are actually seeing.
misreadings: Not a licence to call others blind or to mock religious people
Not a rejection of all ritual; it targets treating ritual reward as the final goal
cautions: Harsh tone; use for self-examination, not as a judgement on the reader's loved ones.
speaks_to: being misled by gurus, influencers or confident experts
not_for: someone already ashamed after being deceived (it can sound like blame)
readers in fresh grief

verified_ref: Mundaka Upanishad 1.2.12 (all editions checked).
translation_note: Accurate. The text says 'a brahmana'; our 'a seeker' generalises (Shankara explains the word as naming those specially fit for total renunciation). 'Śrotriya' = learned in scripture; 'brahma-niṣṭha' = established in Brahman. Madhva's translator renders 'samit-pāṇiḥ' as 'with folded hands' whereas Shankara keeps 'fuel in hand'.
context: Having shown that rituals win only temporary worlds, Angiras says the thoughtful person, after examining those worlds, grows dispassionate because the uncreated cannot be produced by action. Such a person should go humbly to a qualified teacher. The next verse tells the teacher to give the full teaching to a calm, ready student.

key_terms.sense: having examined the worlds built up by action
the unmade is not (gained) by the made
with fuel-sticks in hand (sign of a humble student)
learned in scripture and grounded in Brahman

core_teaching: Whatever is achieved by effort is itself temporary; what is eternal cannot be manufactured. Seeing this, a seeker turns humbly to a teacher who both knows the texts and lives the truth.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. S. Sitarama Sastri (1905)
commentaries.gist: Everything action can do is produce, reach, refine or modify; none of these yields the eternal. Disgusted with such ends, the seeker should go to a teacher, since even a scholar should not seek Brahman-knowledge on his own.

commentaries.who: Madhva school (Dvaita), tr. S. C. Vasu (1909)
commentaries.gist: Renders it as mastering and then letting go of desire for worlds gained by works, because the uncreated world of Brahman is not won through created ones; then approaching an inspired teacher with humility.

practical_reading: Teachers use it when achievement stops satisfying: you cannot build your way to peace, so look for someone wiser and learn. A good mentor needs both knowledge and lived integrity.
misreadings: Not a rejection of work or achievement as such
Not a demand to obey any self-proclaimed guru; the verse specifies learning and real grounding
The word 'brahmana' should not be used to exclude anyone
cautions: The original names a brahmana as the seeker; keep the reading caste-neutral.
Guru language can be exploited; stress the teacher's qualifications.
speaks_to: looking for a mentor or teacher
not_for: someone recovering from abuse by a spiritual teacher
people under financial pressure who need achievement to survive

verified_ref: Mundaka Upanishad 2.2.4 (all editions checked).
translation_note: Accurate. 'Apramattena' = by one who is not heedless (Shankara: free of thirst for external objects, with a concentrated mind). Our line ('focus like an archer... until you and your target become one') is a fair modern paraphrase but drops Om and Brahman; the writer should keep them.
context: In the previous verse Angiras tells the seeker to take up the great weapon of the Upanishad as a bow, fit to it an arrow sharpened by meditation, draw it with a mind absorbed in That, and hit the imperishable. Here he explains the image: Om is the bow, the self the arrow, Brahman the target. The verses after describe Brahman as that in which the worlds are woven.

key_terms.sense: it is to be pierced by one who is undistracted
like the arrow, one becomes one with it

core_teaching: Meditation on Om carries the attention, as a bow sends an arrow, to rest in Brahman; with undistracted focus the self becomes one with its aim. Shankara: the 'hit' is the end of identifying with the body.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. S. Sitarama Sastri (1905)
commentaries.gist: Repeating Om purifies the self so it settles in Brahman unobstructed, as a bow drives an arrow home. The arrow is the supreme self appearing as the individual; the hit is dropping the notion that the body is the self.

commentaries.who: Madhva school (Dvaita), tr. S. C. Vasu (1909)
commentaries.gist: Translates the arrow as the mind and says the one with concentrated thought enters the target; the translator's note reads the verses as teaching hearing, reflection and meditation on Brahman as a method of worship.

practical_reading: Teachers use the archer to teach steady attention: a single point of focus, a support like a mantra or breath, and no distraction. It also applies to work that needs deep focus.
misreadings: Not just a productivity tip; the target in the text is Brahman
Not about aggression or competitiveness
cautions: Low risk. Avoid turning it into pressure to perform.
not_for: someone exhausted and needing rest rather than more focus

verified_ref: Mundaka Upanishad 2.2.8 (all editions checked; Madhva's running number 40).
translation_note: Accurate. 'Parāvara' = both high and low; Shankara: high as cause, low as effect; Madhva: the one to whom even the highest beings are low. Our line 'old deeds lose their grip' is a fair gloss; Shankara specifies that the karma already bearing fruit in this life continues.
context: Angiras has been describing Brahman as the inner controller dwelling in the heart, to be meditated on as Om. This verse states the fruit of seeing it. The next verses describe Brahman as the stainless light in the golden sheath, the light by which sun, moon and fire shine.

key_terms.sense: knot of the heart (desires and ignorance in the mind)
the one who is both high and low (cause and effect)

core_teaching: Directly seeing the highest unties the knot of desire and ignorance, ends doubt, and exhausts accumulated karma. Shankara adds that the karma that has already produced this present life still runs its course.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. S. Sitarama Sastri (1905)
commentaries.gist: The knot is the mass of desires lodged in the intellect, not in the self. On seeing the self as 'I am He', doubts end and stored karma is destroyed, except the karma already bearing fruit as this birth.

commentaries.who: Madhva (Dvaita), tr. S. C. Vasu (1909)
commentaries.gist: Madhva glosses 'parāvara' as Vishnu, compared with whom even the highest beings are low; the translator's notes read the knot as the bonds of ignorance, desire and karma on the soul, cut when the Lord is seen.

practical_reading: Teachers use it for the relief of real clarity: when you truly understand, inner knots and endless second-guessing fall away. It also offers hope that the past need not define you.
misreadings: Not a promise that consequences of past actions vanish instantly in practical life
Not intellectual certainty or winning an argument
cautions: Talk of karma wearing away may raise questions of guilt; keep it hopeful rather than transactional.
not_for: someone using it to dismiss responsibility for recent harm

verified_ref: Mundaka Upanishad 3.1.1 (all editions checked). Also Rig Veda 1.164.20 and Shvetashvatara Upanishad 4.6.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Sayujā sakhāyā' = closely joined companions; 'abhicākaśīti' = looks on, shines. Madhva reads 'svādu' as 'as if sweet' (the soul eats bitter and sweet alike).
context: The third Mundaka opens with this image right after the teaching that the knot of the heart is cut by seeing the highest. The next verse says the bird that eats, sunk in the same tree, grieves at its helplessness, but when it sees the other, the Lord, and his glory, its grief goes. Shankara treats the verse as a summary restatement of the truth from a new angle.
core_teaching: In each of us there is the self that tastes the joys and pains of action, and the witness that only watches. Recognising the witness brings freedom from the eater's sorrow.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. S. Sitarama Sastri (1905)
commentaries.gist: The tree is the body; the eating bird is the individual self tasting pleasure and pain through ignorance; the other is the ever-free Lord who directs by mere presence as witness, as a king rules simply by being there.

commentaries.who: Madhva (Dvaita), tr. S. C. Vasu (1909)
commentaries.gist: The soul eats bitter and sweet fruit alike, as if sweet; the Lord does not eat the soul's karmic fruit and never suffers. The verse shows the soul and God as distinct even while dwelling together.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to teach the observer stance: alongside the part of you caught up in events, there is a part that can watch without being swept away. Mindfulness practice often starts here.
misreadings: Not detachment as coldness toward others
Not a claim that experience doesn't matter
cautions: Low risk. Advaita and Dvaita disagree whether the birds are finally one or two; avoid presenting either as the only reading.
speaks_to: feeling lonely (the companion bird is always there)
not_for: someone dissociating after trauma, where 'just watch' may deepen disconnection

verified_ref: Mundaka Upanishad 3.1.6 (all editions checked). The first words are India's national motto.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Vitataḥ' = spread out, kept open; 'āpta-kāmāḥ' = whose desires are fulfilled. Shankara reads 'truth' as the truthful person: it is the one who speaks truth who wins.
context: Angiras is listing the aids to self-knowledge: truth, austerity, right knowledge and continence (3.1.5). This verse praises truth as the strongest of them. The next verse describes Brahman as vast, self-luminous and near, seen within by the wise.
core_teaching: Truthfulness is the decisive aid on the spiritual path; the truthful prevail, and the path of the sages is kept open by truth. Shankara stresses truthful speech; Madhva reads Truth as the Lord himself.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. S. Sitarama Sastri (1905)
commentaries.gist: It is the person who speaks truth who wins, as the world sees liars defeated by the truthful. Truth keeps the path of the gods open for sages free of deceit, pride and desire.

commentaries.who: Madhva (Dvaita), tr. S. C. Vasu (1909)
commentaries.gist: Satya is Vishnu, called true because he has all good qualities; those opposed to him are 'untrue' and do not reach him. The highest abode of truth is Vishnu's Vaikuntha.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to encourage honesty when lying looks easier: truth builds a road you can keep walking. Integrity is part of spiritual practice, not separate from it.
misreadings: Truth wins in the long run; it is not a promise of quick or worldly victory (our misuse note is right)
Not a licence for blunt cruelty in the name of truth
Not a nationalist slogan in its original setting
cautions: Someone who told the truth and suffered for it may find 'truth always wins' hollow; frame it as the path, not a guaranteed outcome.
speaks_to: temptation to lie or cut corners
not_for: someone punished for honesty and still hurting, without acknowledgement of that cost

verified_ref: Mundaka Upanishad 3.2.2 (all editions checked).
translation_note: Accurate. 'Kṛtātmanaḥ' = one who has realised (Shankara) / whose mind is content (Madhva); 'paryāpta-kāma' = one whose desire is fulfilled (in the self).
context: The second section of the third Mundaka opens by praising those who worship the knower of Brahman without desire. This verse contrasts the person driven by desires with the one whose desires are fulfilled in the self. The next verse says the self is not won by study or intellect but reveals itself to the one it chooses.

key_terms.sense: who desires objects, dwelling on their merits
of one whose desire is fulfilled
of one who has realised the self, made himself whole

core_teaching: Brooding on desires keeps us bound to chase them, life after life; for one fulfilled in the self, desires dissolve even here and now.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. S. Sitarama Sastri (1905)
commentaries.gist: Renouncing desire is the primary aid to liberation. Whoever covets objects, brooding on their virtues, is reborn wherever desire leads; for one whose desire is the self, desires stop arising because their causes are destroyed.

commentaries.who: Madhva school (Dvaita), tr. S. C. Vasu (1909)
commentaries.gist: One who thinks objects of desire are the highest is born where they can be enjoyed; but desires vanish even on earth for one who aspires to the highest and whose mind is content. Direct knowledge alone ends desire entirely.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to show that wanting tends to breed more wanting, while inner contentment loosens desire's grip. Notice which desires you keep feeding by dwelling on them.
misreadings: Not a condemnation of all wanting or of healthy ambition
'Whole in himself' does not mean self-sufficient isolation
cautions: Rebirth is assumed ('born here and there'); keep it gentle for readers who don't hold that belief.
not_for: someone grieving a lost desire (a child, a partner) who may hear 'stop wanting'

verified_ref: Mundaka Upanishad 3.2.4 (all editions checked).
translation_note: Mostly accurate. 'Tapaso vāpy aliṅgāt': Shankara takes tapas as knowledge and liṅga as renunciation (knowledge without sannyasa); Madhva takes aliṅga as 'without scriptural sanction'. Our 'austerity without a true aim' is a neutral middle reading; acceptable with a note. Our line ('whoever strives wisely gets there') drops the condition 'by these means'.
context: The previous verse says the self is not reached by study, intellect or much learning, but by the one it chooses. This verse adds the human side: strength, care and the right kind of discipline are needed. The next verses describe sages who, having attained it, enter the All.

key_terms.sense: by one lacking strength (Shankara: strength born of steady devotion to the self)
nor by austerity (or knowledge) lacking its proper mark

core_teaching: Self-knowledge needs inner strength, attentiveness and the right kind of discipline; whoever strives with these means reaches Brahman's home.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. S. Sitarama Sastri (1905)
commentaries.gist: Strength is that born of steadiness in the self; heedlessness is distraction by attachment to family and possessions; tapas here means knowledge, and its mark is renunciation. With these aids, the knower's self enters Brahman.

commentaries.who: Madhva (Dvaita), tr. S. C. Vasu (1909), with translator's notes
commentaries.gist: The austerity must be sattvic and scripturally sanctioned. Hearing and reflection support devotion but are secondary; the chief means is grace, received by the devotee who strives and prays.

practical_reading: Teachers use it against both laziness and showy austerity: real progress needs inner strength and attentiveness, with practice aimed at the right goal. Effort and grace work together.
misreadings: 'Weak' does not mean physically weak or ill
Not a call to harsh self-mortification
cautions: 'Not won by the weak' can wound someone who is depressed, disabled or exhausted; clarify that strength here is inner resolve.
speaks_to: procrastination in spiritual or personal practice
practice that has become showy or rigid
not_for: someone with depression or chronic illness who already feels weak
a reader in grief

verified_ref: Mundaka Upanishad 3.2.8 (all editions checked).
translation_note: Accurate on Shankara's reading. Madhva reads 'vimuktaḥ' as 'not losing' and holds that rivers and the freed soul keep their identity; our 'merge in the highest' follows Shankara only.
context: The preceding verses describe the sages who know Brahman entering the All at death, their parts returning to their sources. This verse gives the image of rivers entering the sea. The next verse says the knower of Brahman becomes Brahman, crossing grief and sin.

key_terms.sense: the divine Person beyond the beyond (Shankara: beyond the unmanifest)

core_teaching: As rivers lose their separate names in the sea, the knower lets go of the identity built from name and form and reaches the highest. Advaita reads this as merging; Dvaita as reaching God without losing the self.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. S. Sitarama Sastri (1905)
commentaries.gist: As the Ganga and other rivers give up their distinct identity in the sea, the knower, freed from name and form created by ignorance, reaches the self-luminous Person beyond the unmanifest.

commentaries.who: Madhva (Dvaita), tr. S. C. Vasu (1909)
commentaries.gist: Rivers only seem to lose name and form to ordinary eyes; the wind knows each drop and returns it as rain. Likewise the freed soul keeps its individuality; name and form are never actually lost.

practical_reading: Teachers use it for letting go of a small, defensive sense of self and finding belonging in something larger. It can also speak to the ego's fear of losing itself.
misreadings: Not a description of death as annihilation
Not a call to erase one's personality or culture
cautions: Often read at funerals; for fresh grief, 'giving up name and form' may feel like loss of the person; use the Dvaita reading or hold back.
not_for: fresh bereavement unless handled gently
someone fearing loss of self in depression or dissociation

verified_ref: Not part of the Narayana Upanishad. The short Narayana Upanishad (Krishna Yajurveda; tr. K. Narayanasvami Aiyar, Thirty Minor Upanishads, 1914) has five brief sections and contains no such verse, so a '16-17' reference does not exist. The verse is the familiar dhyana (meditation) shloka on Vishnu recited before the Vishnu Sahasranama; its original source was not verified.
attribution_note: Reference and speaker are both wrong: it is a devotional dhyana verse of uncertain origin, not Upanishadic text. Our own our_note already says it is 'appended to printed editions and is not part of the Upanishad's own text'; the ref should not present it as Narayana Upanishad 16-17. Suggest re-labelling as 'Traditional Vishnu dhyana shloka (recited before the Vishnu Sahasranama)'.
translation_note: Translation is accurate to the Sanskrit given: śāntākāram = of peaceful form; bhujaga-śayanam = lying on the serpent (Shesha); padma-nābham = lotus-naveled; gagana-sadṛśam = like the sky; megha-varṇam = cloud-coloured; bhava-bhaya-haram = remover of the fear of worldly existence.
context: The verse is a visualisation to hold in mind before worship or recitation: Vishnu lying on the cosmic serpent, calm, vast as the sky, dark as a rain-cloud, with Lakshmi. It stands outside any narrative and is used at the start of the Vishnu Sahasranama and in daily prayer. The Narayana Upanishad itself is a short prose text on everything coming from and returning to Narayana, and on the eight-syllable mantra 'Om namo Narayanaya'.

key_terms.sense: remover of the fear of worldly existence

core_teaching: A meditation image of God as utterly peaceful even while resting on a serpent, holding up the universe; bowing to him takes away the fear that comes with worldly life.
practical_reading: Commonly recited at the start of prayer or before sleep to settle fear; the image of calm repose on a serpent is often explained by teachers as peace amid danger. (Not sourced to a classical commentary.)
misreadings: Not an Upanishadic statement of doctrine; it is a devotional visualisation
Not a promise that worldly dangers will disappear
cautions: Do not cite it as Upanishad scripture in user-facing text.
Sectarian (Vaishnava) image; fine for devotional plans but label clearly.
speaks_to: anxiety and fear before sleep or exams
wanting a calming image to hold
not_for: plans presenting Upanishadic philosophy
readers expecting a sourced scriptural teaching
research_note: No commentary or reliable published source for the verse's origin was found in this pass (the Wikipedia page on the Vishnu Sahasranama, checked, does not mention it). Recommend re-attributing in data and keeping commentaries empty unless an editor sources it.

verified_ref: Niralamba Upanishad 10 in T. R. Srinivasa Ayyangar's Adyar translation (1941, following Upanishad-brahma-yogin); question 21 in K. Narayanasvami Aiyar's translation (Thirty Minor Upanishads, 1914). Our number 10 matches the Adyar numbering.
attribution_note: The Upanishad is a catechism with no named speakers; 'Teacher -> Seeker' is fine.
translation_note: Accurate. Adyar: jati is not of skin colour, blood, flesh, bone or the self; it is a convention arising from everyday dealings. Aiyar: there is no caste for the self; caste is only conventional.
context: The Niralamba Upanishad opens by promising to explain, in question-and-answer form, what must be known to end suffering. It defines Brahman, Ishvara and the jiva, then says Brahma, Vishnu, Rudra, the gods, humans, women, animals and the castes are all Brahman. This answer on jati comes next; the following questions define karma, knowledge, happiness, heaven and hell.

key_terms.sense: not of the skin, not of the blood

core_teaching: Caste is not in the body or in the self; it is a social convention for practical life. At the level of the self, there is no birth-group at all.

commentaries.who: Upanishad-brahma-yogin (Advaita), as rendered by T. R. Srinivasa Ayyangar (Adyar, 1941)
commentaries.gist: Glosses jati as division based on birth and says it belongs neither to skin colour, blood, flesh, bone nor the self; it is a convention that comes from everyday transactions.

commentaries.who: K. Narayanasvami Aiyar tr., Niralamba Upanishad (1914)
commentaries.gist: Places the answer right after the teaching that gods, humans, women, animals and the castes are all Brahman, with no manyness at all; caste cannot refer to the body and is merely conventional.

practical_reading: Used today to argue that birth-group identity says nothing about a person's worth or inner nature. Teachers apply it against caste prejudice and, by extension, racial or colour prejudice.
misreadings: The text calls caste a convention, not unreal for all purposes; avoid overstating it as a social reform manifesto in its own time
Not a claim that caste discrimination doesn't happen
cautions: Caste is a live and painful issue; do not use the verse to dismiss someone's experience of discrimination ('caste doesn't really exist')
Avoid naming specific castes
not_for: contexts where it would be used to deny lived discrimination

verified_ref: Niralamba Upanishad 16-17 in the Adyar translation (1941); questions 28-29 in Aiyar (1914). Our '17' is approximately right (svarga is 16, naraka 17 in the Adyar numbering).
translation_note: Accurate to our Sanskrit. 'Sat' can mean good people or Brahman (Aiyar gives both). Aiyar's text for naraka has 'association with the false which brings about worldly existence' without 'people'; the Adyar text includes people enamoured of worldly pleasures. Our translation follows the fuller reading.
context: In the same catechism, after defining happiness as knowing Brahman and sorrow as dwelling on worldly objects, the Upanishad defines heaven and hell. It then goes on to bondage (thoughts of 'I' and 'mine') and liberation. The answers keep turning external religious ideas into states of mind and company.

key_terms.sense: association with the good (or with the Real)
association with the unreal world, its objects and people lost in them

core_teaching: Heaven and hell are not only places after death; good company lifts us now, and company sunk in hollow pursuits drags us down.

commentaries.who: Upanishad-brahma-yogin (Advaita), as rendered by T. R. Srinivasa Ayyangar (Adyar, 1941)
commentaries.gist: Companionship with the good is the heavenly state; companionship with people enamoured of the illusory pleasures of worldly life is hell, because it leads toward hell's torments.

commentaries.who: K. Narayanasvami Aiyar tr., Niralamba Upanishad (1914)
commentaries.gist: Translates svarga as association with Sat, noting it can mean good people or Brahman, and naraka as association with what produces worldly existence, the false.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to stress how much the people around us shape our inner life: choose friends and influences that bring out the best in you. It fits advice on friendships, online spaces and habits.
misreadings: Not a licence to look down on or shun people as 'worldly'
Not a denial of afterlife teaching elsewhere; it gives an inner meaning
cautions: Can be used to justify cutting people off harshly; stress choosing influences, not condemning individuals.
not_for: someone isolated with no supportive company, who may feel condemned to 'hell'

verified_ref: Prashna Upanishad 1.2 (all editions checked: S. Sitarama Sastri with Shankara; Vasu with Madhva).
attribution_note: Pippalada to the six seekers (Sukesha, Satyakama, Gargya, Kausalya, Bhargava, Kabandhi). Correct.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Tapas, brahmacarya, śraddhā' = austerity, continence (celibacy), faith; our 'discipline, self-restraint and faith' is acceptable.
context: Six seekers devoted to Brahman come to the sage Pippalada with fuel in hand, hoping he will explain everything. Here he asks them to stay another year with discipline, continence and faith before asking. After the year each asks one question, which gives the Upanishad its six chapters.

key_terms.sense: you will dwell (here) for a year

core_teaching: Deep questions need preparation; the teacher asks for a year of disciplined living first. His 'if we know' shows humility, not doubt.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. S. Sitarama Sastri
commentaries.gist: Though they had already practised austerity, they are to live another year with special care for continence and faith and in service of the teacher. 'If we know' shows the teacher's freedom from conceit, not uncertainty.

commentaries.who: Madhva school (Dvaita), tr. S. C. Vasu (1909), translator's note
commentaries.gist: The 'if' shows the teacher's modesty; the pupil should come without doubting the teacher and serve him, and the teacher must love the pupil.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to value patience and readiness: some answers only make sense after you have lived differently for a while. It also models a teacher who admits limits.
misreadings: Not a demand that anyone wait a year before seeking help
Not an excuse for gatekeeping knowledge
cautions: Celibacy (brahmacarya) may need gentle framing for householders as general self-restraint.
speaks_to: building discipline before a big change
not_for: someone in crisis who needs help now

verified_ref: Prashna Upanishad 1.16 (all editions checked).
attribution_note: Pippalada to Kabandhi Katyayana, end of the first answer. Correct.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Jihmam' = crookedness, 'anṛtam' = untruth, 'māyā' = deceit, dissimulation. Shankara takes this 'world of Brahman' as the lower Brahma-loka reached by the northern path, not final liberation.
context: Kabandhi asked where creatures come from. Pippalada answers with paired principles (life and matter, sun and moon, the two paths after death) and says householders who keep their vows reach the world of the moon. This verse closes the answer: the pure world of Brahman belongs to those free of crookedness, falsehood and deceit.
core_teaching: The pure state belongs to those without crookedness, lies or pretence. Shankara: householders' many dealings make these faults hard to avoid, so the path suits those whose lives remove their causes.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. S. Sitarama Sastri
commentaries.gist: This pure Brahma-loka is for those without the fraud, joking falsehood and dissimulation (showing one face, acting another) that householder dealings breed: celibate students, forest-dwellers and renunciants who combine works with meditation.

commentaries.who: Madhva school (Dvaita), tr. S. C. Vasu (1909)
commentaries.gist: Renders it as the pure Brahma-loka for those with no crookedness, falsehood or dissimulation; the translator's note sums up the first question as a hierarchy of creative pairs under Vishnu.

practical_reading: Teachers use it as a simple integrity check: no twisting, no lying, no pretending. Being the same inside and outside is its own kind of purity.
misreadings: Not a claim that householders cannot be honest
Not a promise of heaven as a reward for good behaviour
cautions: Shankara's view that householder life breeds deceit may feel judgemental to families; present it as a warning about pressures, not a verdict.
not_for: someone consumed by guilt over past dishonesty, without a word on repair

verified_ref: Prashna Upanishad 2.4 (all editions checked).
attribution_note: Pippalada to Bhargava Vaidarbhi. The setting ('the senses boast...') is correct: in 2.2-2.3 the powers claim to uphold the body and Prana warns them.
translation_note: Accurate to Shankara. 'Abhimānāt' = out of pride (Shankara: from indignation at their disbelief); Madhva takes 'abhimāna' as 'the body', so 'rose out of the body'. 'Madhukara-rāja' is the 'king bee' in the text; 'queen' is the modern zoological correction (Madhva's translator also says Queen-bee).
context: Bhargava asked which powers sustain a creature and which is greatest. Pippalada tells a story: space, wind, fire, water, earth, speech, mind, eye and ear each boast that they hold up the body. Breath, the chief, tells them not to be deluded; they don't believe it, so breath begins to leave and all the others are pulled along. Convinced, they praise breath in the hymn that follows.

key_terms.sense: out of pride / indignation (Shankara); 'from the body' (Madhva)
as if rising up to leave

core_teaching: The vital breath is the support of all the faculties; when it goes, everything goes with it. The story teaches humility to the parts that think they run the whole.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. S. Sitarama Sastri
commentaries.gist: Seeing their lack of faith, Prana seemed to rise from the body in indignation; all the others rose and settled with it, as bees follow their king. Giving up disbelief and seeing Prana's greatness, the senses praise it gladly.

commentaries.who: Madhva (Dvaita), as reported in S. C. Vasu's translation (1909)
commentaries.gist: Madhva takes 'abhimāna' to mean the body, not pride; Prana began to go out of the body to convince the doubting powers. The translator sets this against Shankara's 'wounded pride' reading.

practical_reading: Teachers use it for teamwork and humility: the flashy parts depend on a quiet centre that holds everything together. It is also used to introduce breath awareness.
misreadings: Not a medical claim
Not praise of pride; in Shankara's reading breath acts to correct the others' disbelief
cautions: Describes life leaving the body; could touch someone who recently watched a person die.
speaks_to: taking the basics for granted (health, breath, support staff)
not_for: someone who recently sat with a dying person
respiratory illness or ICU contexts

verified_ref: Prashna Upanishad 6.1 (all editions checked).
attribution_note: Sukesha Bharadvaja to Pippalada, recalling his own reply to Prince Hiranyanabha of Kosala. Correct. (S. Sitarama Sastri's translation misprints the prince's name as 'Hiranyagarbha'.)
translation_note: Accurate. 'Samūlo vā eṣa pariśuṣyati' = such a one dries up root and all; Shankara: is destroyed in this world and the next.
context: This opens the last of the six questions. Sukesha tells Pippalada that a Kosala prince once asked him about the person of sixteen parts; he admitted he didn't know rather than bluff, and the prince drove off in silence. Now Sukesha asks Pippalada where that person is. Pippalada answers that the person is right here within (Vasu's Madhva translation: 'in this heart').

key_terms.sense: I cannot (dare not) tell a lie

core_teaching: Honest 'I don't know' is better than an impressive bluff; lying withers a person from the root. The story also shows how hard this knowledge is to get.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. S. Sitarama Sastri
commentaries.gist: The story spurs seekers by showing how hard this knowledge is. Sukesha explains his ignorance so the prince would believe him; a liar is destroyed in both worlds. Knowledge should go to the worthy, and falsehood never be spoken.

commentaries.who: Madhva school (Dvaita), tr. S. C. Vasu (1909), translator's note
commentaries.gist: Gives the same story; the note says this last chapter shows the Lord rules souls even when released, and presents Prana as the great saviour and mediator.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to give permission to say 'I don't know', at work, as a parent, or as a teacher. Integrity costs a moment of embarrassment; lying costs much more.
misreadings: Not shame at not knowing; the point is honesty about it
Not a literal curse that liars will physically wither
cautions: Low risk. Avoid making it a threat ('liars dry up').
speaks_to: parents and teachers asked hard questions
not_for: someone already ashamed of past lies, if presented as a curse

verified_ref: Vajasaneyi Samhita (Shukla Yajurveda) 34.1; the first six verses of book 34 form the 'Shiva Sankalpa' hymn, treated as an Upanishad (Griffith, Texts of the White Yajurveda, 1899).
attribution_note: Speaker 'Seer' is fine. Listener 'God' is loose: the verses address one's own mind in prayer ('may that mind of mine...'), not a deity directly. Suggest listener 'his own mind (prayer)'.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Jyotiṣāṃ jyotir ekam' = the one light of lights; Griffith's note glosses it as the illuminator of all the perceptive senses. 'Śiva-saṅkalpam' = of auspicious resolve, moved by right intention.
context: Book 34 of the White Yajurveda opens with six verses, each ending with the refrain 'may that mind of mine be of auspicious resolve'. This first verse describes the mind as divine, travelling far in waking and in sleep. The following verses praise the mind as the means of sacrifice, the seat of wisdom and memory, and the charioteer of the person.

key_terms.sense: goes far away while one is awake
and returns the same way when one sleeps
far-going, the one light of lights
may that mind of mine have an auspicious resolve

core_teaching: The mind is a powerful, far-roaming light that illumines all the senses; the prayer is that this power be turned to good intentions.

commentaries.who: R. T. H. Griffith, notes to his translation (Texts of the White Yajurveda, 1899)
commentaries.gist: Says the first six verses form a hymn regarded as an Upanishad, named Shivasankalpa from its refrain; glosses the refrain as having an auspicious resolve and the 'one light' as illuminator of the senses.

practical_reading: Used as a morning or bedtime prayer for good intentions; teachers apply it to setting the mind's direction before the day, since the mind will wander anyway.
misreadings: Not a demand to stop the mind from wandering
Not a magic formula to control thoughts
cautions: Low risk. Gentle prayer.
not_for: someone with intrusive thoughts who may feel guilty for 'bad intentions'
research_note: Only Griffith's notes were read. Classical commentaries (Uvata, Mahidhara) exist in Sanskrit but were not consulted; sacred-texts.com (which hosts Griffith) showed a bot challenge, so the archive.org scan was used.

verified_ref: Vajasaneyi Samhita 34.6, last verse of the Shiva Sankalpa hymn (Griffith 1899).
attribution_note: As for up_shiv_sankalp.1: speaker fine; listener is better described as one's own mind in prayer.
translation_note: Accurate. Griffith: controlling men as a skilful charioteer drives fleet horses with reins; dwelling in the heart, agile, most rapid. 'Ajiram' = ageless or agile (both senses are found); our 'ageless' is fine.
context: This closes the six-verse prayer on the mind. After praising the mind as wisdom, memory and the hub in which all knowledge is set like spokes, the hymn ends with the charioteer image. The next verse in the Samhita begins unrelated ritual verses in praise of food.
core_teaching: The mind steers a person the way a charioteer steers horses; since it decides where we go, we pray that it be set on good.

commentaries.who: R. T. H. Griffith, translation and notes (Texts of the White Yajurveda, 1899)
commentaries.gist: Renders the mind as guiding men like a skilful charioteer with reins, dwelling in the heart and swiftest; notes that the six verses are a separate hymn called Shivasankalpa and that the rest of book 34 is a miscellany.

practical_reading: Teachers use the charioteer image for self-direction: the mind holds the reins of your actions, so steady it with good intentions. A short daily prayer for clear direction.
misreadings: Not mind over body in a harsh sense
Not a claim that one can control all outcomes
cautions: Low risk.
speaks_to: students and young adults choosing a direction
not_for: someone blaming themselves for things outside their control
research_note: Only one source read (Griffith). Compare Katha Upanishad 1.3.3-4 for the chariot image (not checked here).

verified_ref: Shvetashvatara Upanishad 1.1 (same in Röer 1853, Müller SBE 15, Varma 1916).
attribution_note: The verse reports what 'the expounders of Brahman' (brahmavādinaḥ) ask one another. Speaker 'Seekers of Brahman -> each other' is right.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Kiṃ kāraṇaṃ brahma' can be read 'What is the cause? Is it Brahman?' (Müller, who says Shankara prefers this) or 'What kind of cause is Brahman?' (Röer, reporting Shankara's alternatives). 'Sukhetareṣu' = in pleasure and its opposite (pain).
context: The Upanishad opens with a group of Brahman-seekers raising the basic questions together. The next verse lists the candidate causes then debated (time, nature, necessity, chance, the elements, the person) and rejects them. Through meditation the sages then see the power of God hidden in its own qualities as the true cause.

key_terms.sense: governed by whom (do we live) in joy and its opposite?

core_teaching: The Upanishad starts from honest, shared questions about origin, sustenance, destiny and why we live through joy and sorrow. Inquiry, not belief, opens the text.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), as reported in Röer's 1853 translation notes
commentaries.gist: 'Kim' may ask what Brahman's nature is, or whether Brahman is a cause at all, and if so whether material, efficient or both. 'Where we rest' means at the world's dissolution.

commentaries.who: Max Müller, SBE 15 (1884), note
commentaries.gist: Translates 'Is Brahman the cause?', saying Shankara himself prefers this when he later recaps the question as 'is Brahman the cause or time and the rest'; notes textual errors in Röer's edition.

commentaries.who: Siddheshwar Varma, The Svetasvatara Upanisad (1916), notes citing commentators
commentaries.gist: Lists three commentarial readings of the first question; observes that we evidently don't control our own joy and sorrow, so some overseer must govern them.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to honour big questions: where did I come from, what sustains me, where am I going, who or what governs my ups and downs. Asking them together, with others, is itself a spiritual act.
misreadings: Not doubt for its own sake; the questions lead to meditation and an answer
Not a fatalistic claim that we have no say in our lives
cautions: Low risk. 'Who governs our sorrows' can raise the problem of suffering; don't force an answer on the reader.
speaks_to: after a major life event that shakes assumptions
not_for: someone in acute grief who needs comfort rather than open questions

verified_ref: Shvetashvatara Upanishad 1.15 (all three editions checked).
translation_note: Accurate. 'Srotaḥsu' = in streams; Müller and Röer take it as dry riverbeds that yield water when dug. 'Satyena tapasā' = by truth and austerity (Röer, following Shankara: austerity as subduing senses and mind; Varma: mental concentration). Our line 'already within; sincere effort brings it out' captures it.
context: The preceding verses compare the self to fire hidden in fire-sticks: present but unseen until drilled out, as meditation on Om draws out the self from the body. This verse gives four more images of something hidden in a substance and drawn out by effort. The next verse says the self pervades all like butter in milk, rooted in self-knowledge and austerity.
core_teaching: The self is already present within, as oil is in seed or fire in wood, but it has to be drawn out by truthfulness and disciplined effort.

commentaries.who: E. Röer tr. (1853), following Shankara's commentary
commentaries.gist: Each image implies a process: pressing the seed, churning the curd, digging the riverbed, rubbing the sticks; likewise the self is perceived within by one who looks with truth and with austerity that subdues senses and mind.

commentaries.who: Max Müller, SBE 15 (1884), notes
commentaries.gist: Explains 'streams' as dry riverbeds that give water when dug; notes the line reads better with the Brahmopanishad's variant, and that the seeker and the self sought are the same.

commentaries.who: Siddheshwar Varma (1916), notes
commentaries.gist: The Supreme Self is to be found not somewhere outside but in one's own mind, obtained by meditation as oil by pressing and fire by friction; tapas here is concentration of mind and senses.

practical_reading: Teachers use it for patience in inner work: what you seek is not missing, only hidden, and steady practice (honesty, discipline, meditation) brings it out the way churning brings out butter.
misreadings: Not 'you already have it, so no effort is needed'
Not harsh asceticism; tapas is focused effort
cautions: Low risk.
not_for: someone exhausted, if 'effort' is stressed over 'already within'

verified_ref: Shvetashvatara Upanishad 3.5 = Vajasaneyi Samhita 16.2 (Shatarudriya) and Taittiriya Samhita 4.5.1.1 (Müller's and Röer's notes).
attribution_note: Seer to Rudra: correct; borrowed from the Shatarudriya hymn.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Aghorā' = not terrible (Röer notes an alternative 'exceedingly terrible'); 'apāpa-kāśinī' = revealing no evil / revealing holiness; 'giriśanta' = mountain-dweller or bringer of happiness from the mountain (Röer and Varma, with Mahidhara agreeing with Shankara on the term).
context: Chapter 3 praises the one Rudra who rules the worlds and asks him for good understanding (3.4). Verses 5-6 are prayers taken from the Yajurveda: show us your kind form, and turn your arrow away from people and creatures. The chapter then shifts to the vast Person who pervades all.

key_terms.sense: revealing no evil, shining with goodness

core_teaching: The same power that can be fearsome has a kind, peaceful face; the devotee asks to be looked on with that face.

commentaries.who: E. Röer tr. (1853), notes following Shankara
commentaries.gist: Rudra here stands for the supreme spirit; notes the verses come from the Vajasaneyi Samhita and that Mahidhara, the Yajurveda commentator, explains 'giriśanta' as Shankara does.

commentaries.who: Max Müller, SBE 15 (1884)
commentaries.gist: Renders it as a prayer to the mountain-dweller to look on us with his most blessed, auspicious, not-terrible form that reveals no evil; cites the Yajurveda parallels.

commentaries.who: Siddheshwar Varma (1916), notes
commentaries.gist: Calls this a prayer for the manifestation of God's benevolent being and for grace bringing all that is good; explains 'giriśanta' as one who spreads happiness, with Kailasa a later association.

practical_reading: Used as a prayer when life feels harsh: asking to see the kind face of what frightens us. Teachers relate it to trusting that even hard forces have a benevolent side.
misreadings: Not a bargain to avoid all misfortune
Not a claim that God is only gentle; the verse acknowledges the fearsome side
cautions: Low risk. Rudra's 'fearsome' side may need a word for readers unfamiliar with it.
not_for: someone who may hear it as a promise that nothing bad will happen

verified_ref: Shvetashvatara Upanishad 3.17. Reading of the last word varies: 'śaraṇaṃ bṛhat' (great refuge) in Müller and Röer; 'suhṛt' (friend) noted as another reading by Varma (1916) and in many modern editions.
translation_note: Our Sanskrit reads 'suhṛt' (friend), which is a recognised variant; Müller ('the great refuge of all') and Röer ('the infinite support') follow 'bṛhat'. Our line ('everyone's refuge and everyone's friend') depends on the variant; our_note already flags this, keep it.
context: The preceding verse, borrowed from the Purusha hymn, says the Supreme has hands, feet, eyes and ears everywhere. This verse corrects any literal reading: he lights up the work of every sense but has no senses himself. The next verse describes the embodied self in the city of nine gates.

key_terms.sense: shining through the qualities (powers) of all the senses

core_teaching: The Lord gives every sense its power without having senses; he rules all yet is also the shelter, and in one reading the friend, of all.

commentaries.who: E. Röer tr. (1853), notes following Shankara
commentaries.gist: He shines through the qualities of the outer senses and of the mind (sound, colour, doubt, decision) yet has none of these organs; renders the close as lord, ruler and infinite support of all.

commentaries.who: Max Müller, SBE 15 (1884)
commentaries.gist: Separate from all senses yet reflecting their qualities, the lord and ruler and great refuge of all; in the neighbouring note, Shankara explains 'ten fingers beyond' as endless or as the heart's position.

commentaries.who: Siddheshwar Varma (1916), notes
commentaries.gist: The verse removes the hint from 3.16 that God literally has hands and feet; he is the life-giver and sole master of the senses, only seeming to have them. Records 'friend' as another reading.

practical_reading: Teachers draw comfort from it: the power behind all things is not distant but a refuge, and in the popular reading a friend. It suits prayers of trust.
misreadings: Not that God is a human-like friend with needs; he is beyond the senses
The 'friend' wording depends on a variant; avoid overstating it as the only reading
cautions: If quoting 'friend', mention it is one reading.
speaks_to: longing for a sense of being held
not_for: readers who need strict textual precision without the variant explained

verified_ref: Shvetashvatara Upanishad 3.20; near-identical to Katha Upanishad 1.2.20 and Taittiriya Aranyaka 10.12 (Müller). Shvetashvatara reads 'akratum ... īśam' where Katha reads 'akratuḥ ... ātmanaḥ'.
translation_note: Our Sanskrit mixes the two recensions ('akratuḥ' from Katha with 'īśam' from Shvetashvatara). Müller and Röer say the Shvetashvatara reads 'akratum', which describes the Lord as desireless (Müller: 'the Lord, the passionless'; Röer: 'devoid of action'), not the seer as free of grasping. Our translation ('one free of grasping sees him') follows the Katha reading. Also 'dhātuḥ prasādāt' = by the Creator's grace (Shvet. reading); Varma records the alternative 'by the clarity of the senses'. Suggest noting the variant in the reading.
context: After describing the all-pervading Person who has no senses yet works through them all, the seer turns inward: this vast reality is also smaller than the smallest and lives in the heart. The next verse is the seer's own testimony: 'I know this unageing, ancient one, the self of all'.

key_terms.sense: subtler than the subtle, greater than the great
set in the cave (of the heart)
desireless, without will or grasping (applied to the seer in Katha, to the Lord in Shvet.)
by the grace of the Creator (or: by the clarity of the senses)

core_teaching: The infinite lives in the heart of every being; seeing it, by grace and with grasping dropped, ends sorrow.

commentaries.who: Max Müller, SBE 15 (1884), translation and note
commentaries.gist: One who has left grief behind sees the majesty of the passionless Lord by the Creator's grace; Müller had to alter his Katha translation because the Shvetashvatara recension reads 'akratum' and 'īśam'.

commentaries.who: E. Röer tr. (1853), following Shankara
commentaries.gist: Renders it as seeing the glorious ruler as devoid of action, by the grace of the creator, and so becoming free from grief; notes the verse is taken from the Katha with different readings.

commentaries.who: Siddheshwar Varma (1916), notes
commentaries.gist: The verse teaches that spiritual vision depends on grace; records both readings of 'dhātu-prasāda', the Creator's grace or the purity of the senses and mind.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to say the sacred is not far away but in your own heart, and that grace and letting go of grasping open the way. It is a verse of hope after sorrow.
misreadings: Grace is not a reward for being good enough (our misuse note is right)
Not passivity: the Katha context pairs it with inner discipline
cautions: Promises freedom from sorrow; for fresh grief present it as a horizon, not a demand to stop grieving.
not_for: someone in acute grief who may hear 'you should be free of sorrow by now'
research_note: Recommend checking our Sanskrit against a standard Shvetashvatara edition: it appears to carry the Katha reading 'akratuḥ'.
