verified_ref: Shvetashvatara Upanishad 4.11 (all three editions).
translation_note: Accurate. 'Yonim yonim adhitiṣṭhati' = presides over every source/womb (Röer: the first producer and the derived producers, a Samkhya reading; Varma: primary and secondary causes). 'Sam ca vi caiti' = comes together and comes apart (dissolves and is created). 'Nicāyya' = having realised, discerned.
context: Just before, the text calls nature (prakriti) maya and the great Lord its wielder, with the world made of his parts. This verse says knowing that one ruler of all sources brings lasting peace. The next verse repeats the earlier prayer to Rudra for good understanding.

key_terms.sense: the one who presides over each and every source
comes together and goes apart (dissolution and creation)

core_teaching: One Lord stands behind every origin, and the whole world gathers into him and comes forth from him; knowing him brings a peace that does not end.

commentaries.who: E. Röer tr. (1853), notes
commentaries.gist: Reads the sources as nature (first producer) and intellect, ego and subtle elements (derived producers), noting the Samkhya colour of the verse; the boon he grants is liberation, the peace absolute.

commentaries.who: Max Müller, SBE 15 (1884)
commentaries.gist: Translates: whoever has discerned the one who rules every germ, in whom all comes together and comes asunder, the blessing-giving adorable god, passes for ever into that peace.

commentaries.who: Siddheshwar Varma (1916), notes
commentaries.gist: He is the independent governor and support of every cause, primary and secondary; notes another commentator reads 'comes together' as 'gains stability'; the peace is final, without return.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to ground peace in a sense of a single source behind life's comings and goings; things gather and scatter, but the ground remains.
misreadings: Not a promise that life's events will become peaceful
Not merely intellectual knowledge of a doctrine
cautions: Low risk.
not_for: someone needing practical help, if offered as a substitute

verified_ref: Shvetashvatara Upanishad 4.14 (all three editions).
translation_note: Accurate. 'Kalilasya madhye' = in the midst of the turbid mass / chaos (Müller 'chaos'; Varma: the dense confused mass of phenomena, or, per another commentator, darkness). 'Śivam' = the kind, auspicious one, Shiva.
context: This verse comes in a run of 'knowing him, one attains...' sayings in chapter 4 (4.11 peace, 4.15 cutting death's bonds, 4.16 freedom from all fetters). Just before, the seer offers worship to the god who rules all two- and four-footed beings. Here he is described as the subtle, many-formed creator in the middle of the world's confusion.

key_terms.sense: in the midst of chaos, the turbid mass
the one who embraces (envelops) the universe

core_teaching: Right in the middle of the world's tangle is the subtle, kind One who made and holds it all; knowing him brings unending peace.

commentaries.who: Max Müller, SBE 15 (1884)
commentaries.gist: Renders 'kalila' as chaos: the subtle, many-formed creator stands amid it and alone wraps the whole world; Müller glosses Shiva as 'the happy one'. Knowing him, one passes into peace for ever.

commentaries.who: Siddheshwar Varma (1916), notes
commentaries.gist: The chaos is the world of appearances, the work of maya, like a fortress hard to overcome, with the Supreme as its untouched witness; another commentator reads it as darkness hiding him through ignorance.

commentaries.who: E. Röer tr. (1853)
commentaries.gist: Renders 'within that which is impervious', glossed as the creation, with the subtle creator enveloping the universe; knowing the blessed one brings absolute peace.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to say peace is found in the middle of chaos, not after it ends: the kind presence is already inside the confusion.
misreadings: Peace here is inner steadiness, not a promise that outside chaos will stop (our misuse note is right)
cautions: Low risk; good for overwhelm.
speaks_to: overwhelm and chaos at work or home
not_for: someone who may feel told their real problems don't matter
research_note: Röer's OCR for this verse is partly garbled; gist kept to what is legible.

verified_ref: Shvetashvatara Upanishad 4.15 (all three editions).
translation_note: Accurate. 'Kāle' = in time; Shankara (per Müller): in former ages; Varma: at the proper time, or during the world's duration. 'Yuktāḥ' = united with (Müller) or concentrated on him in yoga (Röer, Varma).
context: Continuing the chapter's sayings on what knowing the Lord brings, this verse speaks of him as the world's guardian through time, hidden in all beings. The next verse compares him to the fine film on ghee, hidden in all beings, and says knowing him frees one from all fetters.

key_terms.sense: protector of the world in (due) time
sages and gods united with (or absorbed in) him

core_teaching: The Lord guards the world through time and is hidden in every being; sages and gods find their essence in him, and knowing him cuts through the bonds of death.

commentaries.who: Max Müller, SBE 15 (1884), with Shankara's gloss in note
commentaries.gist: Shankara takes 'in time' as in former ages; sages and deities are 'united' in him because they find their true essence in Brahman. Knowing him cuts death's fetters.

commentaries.who: Siddheshwar Varma (1916), notes
commentaries.gist: The verse points to the great sages who realised the Supreme and adds that we too, by the same methods, can be freed; the noose of death is glossed as darkness, ignorance, maya.

commentaries.who: E. Röer tr. (1853)
commentaries.gist: Renders it as the preserver at the due time, concealed in all beings, with whom the Brahma-seers and deities are united by concentration; knowing him cuts the bonds of death.

practical_reading: Teachers use it for steadiness about time and mortality: a guardian presence runs through the ages and through every being, and knowing it loosens the fear of death.
misreadings: Not a promise of physical immortality
Not a promise that loved ones will be protected from harm
cautions: Mentions death directly; for the recently bereaved, 'cutting death's noose' can feel hollow.
not_for: fresh grief after a death, unless handled carefully

verified_ref: Shvetashvatara Upanishad 4.21 (all three editions).
translation_note: Accurate. 'Dakṣiṇaṃ mukham': Shankara (per Röer) = auspicious, or southern (right-facing); Müller: gracious, noting the readings invigorating or turned south. 'Bhīruḥ' = fearful (Varma: afraid of birth and death).
context: The preceding verses say no one can grasp him above, across or in the middle, no likeness of him exists, and he is known only in the heart. Here the seer turns to personal prayer: someone afraid comes to the Unborn and asks to be protected by his kind face. The next verse is a Vedic prayer for family and livestock.
core_teaching: Fear can be the doorway to refuge: recognising the Unborn, one who is afraid turns to him and asks for protection by his gracious face.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), as reported in Röer's notes (1853)
commentaries.gist: 'Dakṣiṇa' means either auspicious or southern, the face turned to the south; Röer adds that the person is perturbed by the misery of the world.

commentaries.who: Max Müller, SBE 15 (1884)
commentaries.gist: Translates it as someone coming near trembling with the words 'Thou art unborn' and praying that Rudra's gracious face protect him for ever; notes the alternative senses of 'dakṣiṇa'.

commentaries.who: Siddheshwar Varma (1916), notes
commentaries.gist: This verse and the next are prayers, since freedom from evil and reaching God depend on grace; the fearful one fears birth and the rest and turns to Rudra, destroyer of pain.

practical_reading: A prayer for anyone afraid. Teachers use it to say fear does not disqualify you; it can be what brings you to ask for help.
misreadings: A prayer for protection, not a guarantee that nothing bad will happen (our misuse note is right)
Not a replacement for medical, legal or emotional help
cautions: Very suitable for anxious readers; avoid implying that prayer alone will solve a crisis.
not_for: someone in immediate danger who needs practical help first

verified_ref: Shvetashvatara Upanishad 4.22 = Rig Veda 1.114.8; also Taittiriya Samhita 4.5.10.3 and Vajasaneyi Samhita 16.16 (Müller's note).
translation_note: Accurate. 'Toke tanaye' = offspring and descendants (Röer: children and grandchildren); 'bhāmitaḥ' = in anger. Müller notes the closing words vary: Shankara reads 'sadasi' (in the assembly), other commentators 'sadam it' (always).
context: This closes chapter 4 right after the prayer of the frightened devotee. It is an old Rig Vedic prayer to Rudra not to harm children, lives, cattle or warriors, offered by people bringing oblations. Chapter 5 then turns to knowledge and ignorance in the imperishable Brahman.

key_terms.sense: (harm us) not in our children and grandchildren

core_teaching: A parent's and community's prayer: spare our children, our lives and livelihood; we keep calling on you.

commentaries.who: Max Müller, SBE 15 (1884), note
commentaries.gist: Lists the Rig Veda and Samhita parallels and variant readings; notes 'sadasi' in the Shvetashvatara seems to rest on Shankara alone, while Shankarananda and Vijnanatman read 'sadam it', always.

commentaries.who: E. Röer tr. (1853)
commentaries.gist: Renders it as a plea not to injure children, grandchildren, lives, cows or horses, nor slay valiant men in anger, since the worshippers always invoke Rudra with oblations.

commentaries.who: Siddheshwar Varma (1916), notes
commentaries.gist: Treats it with 4.21 as a prayer depending on God's grace, and glosses the grammar: prohibitive forms meaning 'do not destroy', 'bhāmita' as exasperated, worshippers 'full of oblations'.

practical_reading: Used by parents praying for their children's safety, and in times of illness or danger to family.
misreadings: Not a promise of a particular outcome (our misuse note is right)
Not a picture of an arbitrary angry god to be bribed
cautions: Mentions harm to children; may be very painful for parents who have lost a child or whose child is seriously ill
Does not replace medical help
not_for: bereaved parents
parents of a child in critical care, unless chosen by them

verified_ref: Shvetashvatara Upanishad 6.11 (all three editions).
translation_note: Accurate. 'Cetā' = the conscious one, perceiver (Müller notes all manuscripts read 'cetā' not 'cettā'); 'kevalaḥ' = alone, absolute; 'nirguṇaḥ' = without qualities (Röer: without the three gunas).
context: In the last chapter the seer describes the one God who, like a spider spinning thread, covers himself with what comes from nature. This verse is the fullest statement of that God as the hidden self in all beings. The next verse says the wise who see him in themselves have eternal happiness, not others.

key_terms.sense: the inner self of all beings
witness, conscious, alone and beyond qualities

core_teaching: One God is hidden in every being as its inner self: the witness of all actions, pure awareness, untouched by qualities.

commentaries.who: Max Müller, SBE 15 (1884), with Shankara's gloss on the next verse
commentaries.gist: Translates the list of epithets; on the following verse notes Shankara's view that actions belong to the organs of living beings and do not affect the Highest Self, which stays passive.

commentaries.who: Siddheshwar Varma (1916), notes
commentaries.gist: Each epithet answers an objection: 'one' against many souls, 'self-luminous' against materialism, 'hidden' because maya veils him, 'all-pervading' and 'inner self' so that pervading does not mean a second thing.

commentaries.who: E. Röer tr. (1853)
commentaries.gist: Glosses 'mere thinking' as thought without any particular thought, and 'without qualities' as free of the three gunas; Röer reads the context through Samkhya, where only nature acts and the soul witnesses.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to ground respect for every being (the same divine is hidden in all) and to describe the inner witness that watches without being stained by what happens.
misreadings: Not pantheism in the sense that every act is divine or excused
'Overseer of actions' is not a surveillance image
cautions: Low risk.
not_for: someone who may hear 'witness' as being told to detach from pain they need to feel

verified_ref: Shvetashvatara Upanishad 6.18 (all three editions).
attribution_note: Seer (first person, 'I take refuge') to the seekers/God: fine.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Ātma-buddhi-prakāśam' = who lights up the understanding of the self; Müller notes manuscripts vary between '-prakāśam' and '-prasādam' (who makes it clear/gracious), and that Shankarananda explains it as the witness of one's own understanding. 'Brahmā' here is the creator god, not Brahman.
context: Near the end of the Upanishad, after describing the Lord as the eternal among eternals and the light by which all shines, the seer makes a personal act of refuge as one seeking liberation. The next verse describes that God as partless, actionless, peaceful and the last bridge to immortality.

key_terms.sense: who first creates Brahma (the creator god)
and sends (hands) the Vedas to him

core_teaching: The source of all creation and revelation is also the light that makes self-knowledge dawn in us; the seeker, longing for freedom, takes refuge there.

commentaries.who: Max Müller, SBE 15 (1884), notes reporting commentators
commentaries.gist: Records the manuscript variants 'light of his own thoughts' and 'grace of his own thoughts'; Shankarananda explains the former as the witness of one's own understanding.

commentaries.who: Siddheshwar Varma (1916), notes
commentaries.gist: The prayer shows God's grace as a means to true knowledge, as in chapter 3; he is the illuminator of spiritual understanding, and 'creates' can mean in every cycle of creation.

commentaries.who: E. Röer tr. (1853)
commentaries.gist: Renders it as the seeker approaching the protection of the God who manifests knowledge of himself, who at the start of creation made Brahma and gave him the Vedas.

practical_reading: Teachers use it as a closing prayer of surrender after effort: having inquired and practised, the seeker asks for the light of understanding. It can be recited before study or meditation.
misreadings: Refuge is not a substitute for effort (our misuse note is right)
'Brahma' is the creator deity, not Brahman, the absolute
cautions: Low risk.
not_for: someone who wants purely secular framing

verified_ref: Skanda Upanishad 1 (Krishna Yajurveda; K. Narayanasvami Aiyar, Thirty Minor Upanishads, 1914; T. R. Srinivasa Ayyangar, Adyar, 1941).
attribution_note: No named speaker; a first-person declaration addressed to Mahadeva. Aiyar's note says Skanda (represented by Sanatkumara) is associated with it. 'Seer -> Mahadeva' is fine.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Acyuto'smi' = I am unfallen/unswerving (Adyar: 'I have not swerved from the path'; Aiyar: 'indestructible'). Note the pun: Achyuta is also a name of Vishnu, and the Upanishad goes on to say Shiva and Vishnu are one. 'Vijñāna-ghana' = a mass of pure knowing.
context: The Skanda Upanishad opens with this thanksgiving and goes on to say that when the inner instruments fall away, only consciousness remains, which is Hari, Mahadeva and Brahman alike. It declares that Shiva and Vishnu are one, that the jiva is Shiva, and repeats the 'body is a temple' verses found in the Maitreya Upanishad.

key_terms.sense: I am unfallen, unshaken (also: I am Achyuta)
by a mere trace of (your) compassion
a solid mass of pure consciousness

core_teaching: Even a trace of the Lord's grace is enough to make one steady and to reveal one's true nature as pure consciousness, one with Shiva; nothing is higher than that.

commentaries.who: Upanishad-brahma-yogin (Advaita), as rendered by T. R. Srinivasa Ayyangar (Adyar, 1941)
commentaries.gist: Frames the verse as the knower's realisation of identity between Brahman and the self: by a bit of grace he has not swerved from the path, is wisdom itself, and is Shiva, Brahman not different from the inmost self.

commentaries.who: K. Narayanasvami Aiyar tr., Skanda Upanishad (1914)
commentaries.gist: Renders the opening as 'I am indestructible through a small portion of thy grace'; notes the text's identification of Shiva and Vishnu would shock sectarian partisans who quarrel over supremacy.

practical_reading: Teachers use it as a gratitude prayer: a little grace is enough to steady us. It also models a non-sectarian devotion that sees Shiva and Vishnu as one.
misreadings: Not ego inflation ('I am God, so I am above others')
Not a sectarian claim of Shiva over Vishnu; the text identifies them
cautions: Strongly non-dual; some devotional readers may need the grace framing emphasised.
not_for: readers with a strictly dualist devotional view, without explanation

verified_ref: Taittiriya Upanishad 1.9.1 (Shiksha Valli, anuvaka 9; Mahadeva Sastri 1903). Our Sanskrit gives the first four of twelve pairs.
attribution_note: No named speaker; 'Teacher -> Students' is fine.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Ṛta' = right (Shankara: already explained earlier; Sayana: rightly thinking out the word that fits the fact); 'satya' = truth or truthful speech; 'tapas' = austerity; 'dama' = restraint of the outer senses. 'Svādhyāya-pravacane' = study and teaching (or daily recitation).

Lesson 9 guards against thinking meditation makes ordinary duties unnecessary: it lists right conduct, truth, austerity, restraint, calm, the sacred fires, guests, social duties and raising children, each paired with 'and study and teaching'. key_terms.sense: right, order; right thought and speech
study (of one's Veda) and teaching (or recitation)

core_teaching: Every duty in life should be kept company by continued learning and sharing what one learns; study is not a phase that ends.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: Study and teaching are repeated with every duty to show they must be pursued with special care while all the others are done, since knowledge of the Veda, on which the highest good depends, comes only through study.

commentaries.who: Sayana's commentary (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: A seeker of liberation cannot rely on contemplation alone; he must also practise right speech, study and teaching. Even a renunciant should not give up study; neglect obstructs meditation.

practical_reading: Teachers use it for lifelong learning alongside every role: keep studying and keep sharing what you know, whether you are working, parenting or caring for others.
misreadings: Not a claim that study alone is enough
Not limited to Vedic study in a modern reading, but don't erase its original meaning
cautions: The full list includes begetting children; avoid quoting that part to readers facing infertility.
not_for: someone overwhelmed by obligations who may hear another 'should'

attribution_note: The teacher's address to the departing student: correct.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Anuśāsti' = instructs, exhorts; 'satyaṃ vada' = speak the truth; 'dharmaṃ cara' = practise dharma; 'svādhyāyān mā pramadaḥ' = do not be negligent of study.
context: This opens the teacher's famous graduation address in the Shiksha Valli, given when the student has learned the Veda and is about to return home to married life. key_terms.sense: live by dharma, do what is right

core_teaching: As a student goes out into life, the teacher's first counsel is: speak the truth, do what is right, and never stop learning.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: Speak what you know by proper evidence and what is fit to say. A student should not leave the teacher's house without inquiring into dharma; the teacher now explains the meaning of what was learned by heart.

commentaries.who: Sureshvara's Vartika (Advaita), notes marked (S.) in A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: Truth-speaking means saying a thing as it was perceived, without hypocrisy or intent to harm; dharma means the prescribed rites such as the fire offering.

commentaries.who: Sayana's commentary (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: Truth-speaking stands for the related virtues too, such as non-harming and not stealing; the two short commands together mean all scriptural duties should be observed.

practical_reading: Teachers use it as advice for any graduation or new beginning: be honest, act rightly, keep learning. Often quoted at convocations.
misreadings: Not a set of rigid rules; it's a summary of values
Truth here includes not harming, not just blunt factual speech
cautions: Low risk.

verified_ref: Taittiriya Upanishad 1.11.1 (Mahadeva Sastri para 3).
translation_note: Accurate. 'Prajā-tantuṃ mā vyavacchetsīḥ' = do not cut the thread of offspring; 'kuśala' = welfare, self-preservation (Shankara); 'bhūti' = prosperity, well-being. Our 'Do not drift' for 'na pramaditavyam' is good.
context: Continuing the graduation address: after paying the teacher a fitting fee, the student should marry and continue the family line. key_terms.sense: having brought the teacher the wealth he values
one must not be careless, must not swerve

core_teaching: A good life keeps several threads unbroken: gratitude to teachers, family, truth, rightness, health and safety, prosperity, and continued learning and teaching.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: 'Swerving' from truth forbids even an untruth said through forgetfulness. One must not neglect acts for self-preservation (welfare) nor auspicious acts for prosperity; after paying the teacher, marry with his leave and continue the line.

commentaries.who: Sayana's commentary (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: Self-preservation has physical means like medicine and ritual means; wealth likewise. Health and wealth must not be neglected, since without them one cannot do the works that lead toward liberation.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to show the tradition values health, safety and prosperity, not only renunciation: take care of yourself and your livelihood while keeping truth and learning.
misreadings: Not a command that everyone must have children
Not a licence for greed; prosperity sits alongside truth and dharma
cautions: 'Do not cut off the line of your family' can hurt readers facing infertility, child-free by choice, or LGBTQ+; Shankara even mentions rites to obtain a son. Consider omitting that clause in readings
Gender assumptions (son, line of descent) need neutral framing
speaks_to: neglecting health or finances for work
not_for: readers struggling with infertility or pregnancy loss

translation_note: Accurate. 'Mātṛ-devo bhava' = be one for whom the mother is a deity. The first clause ('devapitṛkāryābhyāṃ na pramaditavyam') ends the preceding list in Mahadeva Sastri's paragraphing; fine to keep together.

key_terms.sense: duties to the gods and ancestors
let your mother be a god to you
let your father be a god to you
let your teacher be a god to you
let the guest be a god to you

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: Mother, father, teacher and guest are to be worshipped as deities, not regarded as mere human beings.

commentaries.who: Sayana's commentary (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: Worship your mother as you would a deity such as Rudra, Vishnu or Vinayaka. Rites for the gods include vratas taught in the Puranas; for ancestors, the annual ceremonies.

practical_reading: Teachers use it for gratitude and respect toward parents, teachers and anyone who comes to your door; 'Atithi Devo Bhava' is also India's hospitality motto.
misreadings: Honouring parents does not mean accepting mistreatment or giving up your conscience (our misuse note is right; the very next verse limits following elders to their good conduct)
Not idol-worship of people
cautions: Painful for those with abusive, absent or deceased parents; pair it with the next verse's limit
For those whose parents have died, frame as remembrance

someone estranged for their safety

verified_ref: Taittiriya Upanishad 1.11.2 (Mahadeva Sastri paras 5-6).
attribution_note: Teacher to graduating student: correct. The setting 'the teacher's surprising humility' fits.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Anavadyāni karmāṇi' = blameless acts; 'yāny asmākaṃ sucaritāni' = whatever are our good deeds; 'no itarāṇi' = not the others. Our translation omits the 'not others' after the second sentence (it begins the next verse in our data).
context: Right after telling the student to honour parents and teachers as gods, the teacher limits it: follow only blameless actions, and only the good conduct of your teachers, not the rest. The address continues with how to treat people better than oneself and how to give.
core_teaching: Even revered elders and teachers should be imitated only in what is good; the student keeps his own moral judgement.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: Do only acts free from blame and sanctioned by the practice of the wise; follow the teachers' own good conduct where it agrees with scripture, not their contrary acts, even though teachers do them.

commentaries.who: Sayana's commentary (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: Follow teachers in qualities like fearlessness, not in arrogance. Parashurama obeyed his father by killing his mother: copy the obedience, never the killing. Apply the same test to all custom.

commentaries.who: Sureshvara's Vartika (Advaita), notes marked (S.) in A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: Avoid evil acts, and even acts open to the least suspicion of evil, though practised by the wise; follow the teachers only where they accord with scripture and the practice of the good.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to say respect is not blind obedience: learn from elders' virtues, not their faults. It is a healthy counterweight to 'treat your parents as god'.
misreadings: Not permission to dismiss elders whenever convenient
Not a rejection of tradition
cautions: The Parashurama example in Sayana mentions matricide; don't quote it in a reading for distressed readers.
speaks_to: disillusion with a mentor or parent

verified_ref: Taittiriya Upanishad 1.11.3 (Mahadeva Sastri paras 6 end, 7-8). Our Sanskrit begins with the tail 'no itarāṇi' of the previous sentence.
translation_note: Mostly accurate. 'Āsane na praśvasitavyam' has two readings in Shankara: offer them a seat and relieve their fatigue (our 'seat and refreshment'), or don't so much as breathe (don't interrupt) when they sit in assembly. 'Ye ke cāsmac chreyāṃso brāhmaṇāḥ' = brahmanas better than us; our 'whoever are better than us' drops 'brahmanas'. 'Śriyā deyam' = give with liberality / according to means; 'bhiyā deyam' is literally 'give with fear' (Shankara; Sayana: fear of sin), so our 'Give with respect' softens it; suggest 'with humility' or 'with awe'. 'Saṃvidā' = with friendliness (Shankara) or with understanding.
context: Continuing the address: after limiting imitation to good conduct, the teacher says how to treat learned people better than oneself, then gives the six-fold teaching on giving. Next he says what to do when unsure about right action.

key_terms.sense: give generously, according to one's means
give with fear (awe, fear of wrongdoing)

core_teaching: Honour those wiser than you, and give in the right spirit: with faith, generosity, modesty, a sense of awe, and understanding.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: Honour superior brahmanas with seats and relieve their fatigue, or keep silent in their assembly and just grasp what they say. Give only with reverence, never with irreverence; give liberally, with modesty, with fear, with friendliness.

commentaries.who: Sayana's commentary (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: Read with Gita 17: giving to show off wealth is tamasic, from shame before equals rajasic, from fear of sin sattvic. Or the whole passage is about sattvic giving: give in proportion to your means.

commentaries.who: Sureshvara's Vartika (Advaita), notes marked (S.) in A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: In their discourses do not hurry to speak; grasp the essence of what they say and never contradict them even if you could.

practical_reading: Teachers use it for the ethics of giving today: give respectfully and humbly, in proportion to your means, aware of the person you give to. And listen more than you talk around people wiser than you.
misreadings: Not 'give out of fear of punishment' in a modern anxious sense
'Better than us' was about learned brahmanas; apply it to the wise of any background, not as caste deference
cautions: Caste wording in the original ('brahmanas'); keep the reading inclusive.
not_for: someone in financial hardship who may feel pressure to give

verified_ref: Taittiriya Upanishad 1.11.3-4 (Mahadeva Sastri paras 9-11).
translation_note: Accurate. 'Saṃmarśinaḥ' = thoughtful, competent to judge; 'yuktāḥ' = devoted (Shankara: well-versed); 'āyuktāḥ' = not directed by others (independent); 'alūkṣāḥ' = not harsh; 'abhyākhyāteṣu' = regarding people accused (suspected of wrongdoing). The text says 'brahmanas there'; our 'thoughtful people there' generalises.
context: Near the end of the graduation address the teacher admits that rules will not cover every case. When unsure about an action or about conduct, follow the thoughtful, independent, gentle people around you who care about what is right; do the same in dealing with people under accusation. The address closes: this is the instruction, the teaching, the secret of the Veda.

key_terms.sense: doubt about an action / doubt about conduct
devoted and self-directed (not pushed by others)

core_teaching: When rules run out, look to people who are thoughtful, independent, kind and committed to the right, and act as they would, including in judging the accused.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: In doubt about a rite or custom, act as the brahmanas of that country and age would: able to judge, well-versed, not driven by others, not cruel, seeking dharma, unswayed by desire. Likewise toward people suspected of wrongdoing.

commentaries.who: Sayana's commentary (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: Gives examples of real doubts: contradictory rules on timing of rites, regional customs such as cross-cousin marriage or eating meat. In such cases follow the wise of your own place and time who are free of attachment and aversion.

practical_reading: Teachers use it for moral uncertainty: find wise, kind and independent-minded people and ask how they would act. It also counsels fairness and restraint toward someone accused.
misreadings: Not 'follow the crowd' or local majority opinion; the qualities named are demanding
Not deference to a caste group; in a modern reading, the qualities are what matter
cautions: Original names brahmanas as the reference group; keep inclusive.
speaks_to: how to treat someone accused or in scandal
not_for: someone surrounded only by harsh or manipulative 'advisers'

verified_ref: Taittiriya Upanishad 2.7.1 (Brahmananda Valli, anuvaka 7; para 2 in Mahadeva Sastri).
attribution_note: No named speaker; 'Teacher -> Students' is fine.
translation_note: 'Sukṛtam' is mistranslated as 'well made'. In context (2.7 begins: Brahman made itself by itself, hence it is called su-kṛtam, 'self-made') it means 'that which is self-made', the self-caused (Mahadeva Sastri: 'the self-cause'). Suggested: 'That which is self-made is indeed the essence (rasa). Having found that essence, one becomes joyful.' Our our_note already has this right; fix the translation.
context: Anuvaka 7 opens by saying that in the beginning was non-being, from which being arose; that made itself, so it is called self-made. This verse says that self-made reality is rasa, the essence or 'flavour' that makes life sweet, and that getting it brings joy. The next lines ask who could even breathe if this bliss were not in the space of the heart.

key_terms.sense: He (That) is indeed the essence, the flavour

core_teaching: The self-existent reality is the very essence and sweetness of life; whoever finds it becomes joyful. Joy comes from this source, not from objects.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: Brahman exists because it is rasa, what gives satisfaction. Desireless sages, owning no outer sources of pleasure, are seen full of joy as if they had them; Brahman alone is their source of joy.

commentaries.who: Sureshvara's Vartika (Advaita), notes marked (S.) in A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: Brahman is the supreme essence in a creation that is flavourless in itself; by this rasa the world appears flavourful. For those who have realised the Self, this bliss is direct experience, not inference.

commentaries.who: Sayana's commentary (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: Brahman is called rasa because it is to be relished with love; people love dharma only as a means to heaven, but Brahman is loved for itself, so it must be bliss itself.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to say the deepest joy is not borrowed from things: the sweetness we taste in life comes from a source within, which is why contented people can be happy with little.
misreadings: Not hedonism ('life is about pleasure')
Not a claim that ordinary joys are worthless; they are drops of the same bliss
cautions: For someone in depression, 'joy is within' can feel like an accusation; offer gently.
not_for: clinical depression, without care

verified_ref: Taittiriya Upanishad 2.8.1-2 (Brahmananda Valli, anuvaka 8; paras 2-3 and following in Mahadeva Sastri).
translation_note: Accurate. 'Āśiṣṭhaḥ' = quickest, most active (alternatively 'best eater', per the commentary); 'akāma-hata' = not struck by desire. The joy ladder continues a hundredfold up to Brahma's bliss.
context: Anuvaka 8 opens with the gods and natural forces moving out of fear of Brahman. Then it announces an inquiry into bliss: take the happiest imaginable human (young, good, learned, quick, steady, strong, owning the whole earth's wealth) as one unit, and multiply a hundredfold step by step up to the bliss of Brahma. At every step, a learned person free of desire is said to have that same bliss.

key_terms.sense: and (so too) of the learned one untouched by desire

core_teaching: Even the greatest worldly happiness is a small measure compared with the bliss available as desire thins; a wise person free of craving already has the higher joys.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: The question is whether Brahman's bliss is produced by contact, like worldly pleasure, or is inherent. Worldly pleasure is a fragment of Brahman's bliss, growing a hundredfold at each level as ignorance, desire and karma lessen.

commentaries.who: Sureshvara's Vartika (Advaita), notes marked (S.) in A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: Whatever admits of more and less must culminate in something limitless; so ordinary bliss, raised step by step, points to the immeasurable bliss, taught for those whose gaze is turned outward.

commentaries.who: Sayana's commentary (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: Explains each qualification: youth because children and the old can't enjoy; good because a hostile youth suffers; learned, prompt, steady and strong, since lacking any of these would spoil enjoyment.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to put success in perspective: imagine having everything (youth, health, learning, wealth) and the text says a person free of craving already has more. Contentment outweighs accumulation.
misreadings: Not a put-down of health, learning or wealth; they define the unit of joy
Not literal arithmetic of happiness
cautions: The ideal is a 'young man'; keep the reading gender- and age-neutral.
not_for: someone in poverty or illness who may feel their lack is being idealised

verified_ref: Taittiriya Upanishad 2.9.1 (opening of anuvaka 9 of the Brahmananda Valli).
translation_note: Accurate. 'Kutaścana' = from anywhere at all.
context: After the hundredfold ladder of bliss, anuvaka 9 opens with this verse, which the commentary treats as summing up the teaching that Brahman is beyond speech and thought. It is followed by the sentences on the knower no longer being tormented by regret over good left undone or wrong done.

key_terms.sense: not reaching it, together with the mind
the one who knows the bliss of Brahman

core_teaching: The bliss of Brahman is beyond words and thought; whoever knows it as their own self has nothing left to fear.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: Words denote conditioned things and fail to reach the unconditioned non-dual bliss; the mind, which moves with words, turns back too. The knower of this bliss as the self fears nothing.

commentaries.who: Later Advaita gloss following Shankara's in Mahadeva Sastri (1903), probably Sayana
commentaries.gist: If Brahman is beyond words, how does scripture teach it? Words like 'That thou art' remove ignorance without naming Brahman directly, as calling a sleeper's name wakes him without describing him.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to say the deepest reality is felt rather than explained, and that touching it dissolves fear. Silence and contemplation can go where explanations can't.
misreadings: Not anti-intellectual; words are still used to point
Fearlessness is not recklessness
cautions: Low risk; good for anxiety. Avoid implying that a fearful reader 'doesn't know' enough.
not_for: someone needing concrete practical help

verified_ref: Taittiriya Upanishad 2.9.1 (continued; para 2 of anuvaka 9 in Mahadeva Sastri).
translation_note: Accurate. 'Na tapati' = does not burn, torment. Shankara sets the scene at the approach of death, when such regrets torment people.
context: Right after 'the knower of Brahman's bliss fears nothing', an objection is raised: surely there is fear about one's good and bad deeds? The text answers that such regrets do not burn the knower. The next sentences say the knower treats both good and evil as the self and is strengthened, not weakened, by them.

key_terms.sense: why did I not do good?

core_teaching: For one who knows the self, the burning regret over good undone and wrong done falls away, because the self is not the doer whose account is being kept.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: As death approaches a person is tormented by 'why didn't I do right? why did I do the forbidden?', fearing hell. These two do not afflict the knower of Brahman as they afflict one who does not know.

commentaries.who: Sureshvara's Vartika (Advaita), notes marked (S.) in A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: One who knows the self as non-agent is untouched, since the fruit of action belongs to the agent. Such regrets overtake the ignorant in their last moments; the knower burns good and evil in the fire of knowledge.

commentaries.who: Sayana's commentary (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: Everyone near death regrets merit not earned in youth and sins committed; such thoughts trouble all others but do not assail one who has known Brahman.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to release crippling guilt and regret so a person can live and act well now. Freedom from self-torment is the ground for genuine amends.
misreadings: Not a licence to stop caring about harm done (our misuse note is right)
Not moral indifference; the commentators assume ethical life precedes this knowledge
cautions: The commentaries set it at the moment of death; avoid with readers facing terminal illness unless chosen
Could be misused to excuse an abuser's lack of remorse
not_for: someone who has recently harmed another and hasn't made amends
victims, if read as their abuser's absolution

verified_ref: Taittiriya Upanishad 3.1.1 (Bhriguvalli, anuvaka 1; paras 1-4 in Mahadeva Sastri).
attribution_note: Varuna to his son Bhrigu: correct.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Adhīhi bhagavo brahma' = Sir, teach me Brahman; 'vijijñāsasva' = seek to know thoroughly; 'tapas' = Shankara: concentration of the outer and inner instruments.
context: The third section opens with a story: Bhrigu asks his father Varuna to teach him Brahman. Varuna names food, breath, eye, ear, mind and speech as doors, and gives a definition: that from which beings are born, by which they live, into which they return. Bhrigu goes off to practise tapas and comes back with successive answers: food, breath, mind, understanding, and finally bliss.

key_terms.term: annaṃ prāṇaṃ cakṣuḥ śrotraṃ mano vācam
key_terms.sense: food, breath, eye, ear, mind, speech (gateways)
that from which these beings are born

core_teaching: Brahman is that from which all beings come, by which they live, and into which they return; a good teacher points the way, and the student must discover it through his own disciplined reflection.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: Varuna names food and the senses as gateways to perceiving Brahman, then gives its definition: that with which beings stay one at birth, life and dissolution. Seek to reach Brahman so defined through those gateways.

commentaries.who: Sureshvara's Vartika (Advaita), notes marked (S.) in A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: The story shows Brahma-vidya comes only through a teacher, approached with faith and a pure mind; Bhrigu asks after turning away from every pleasure short of liberation.

commentaries.who: Sayana's commentary (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: Upanishad stories like this extol the teaching rather than serve ritual recitation; Varuna, a most friendly teacher, gives the definition without being asked, likening beings to waves and foam in one ocean.

practical_reading: Teachers use it for learning by discovery: the best teachers give pointers and a question, then let you work it out. Also a model of a parent who teaches by guiding rather than telling.
misreadings: Not that food is God; food is the first gateway
Not a refusal by the father to teach
cautions: Mentions death ('into which they enter at death'); mild.
speaks_to: big-picture questions about origin and purpose

verified_ref: Taittiriya Upanishad 3.2.1 (Bhriguvalli, anuvaka 2; para 3 in Mahadeva Sastri); repeated in anuvakas 3-5.
translation_note: Accurate. Mahadeva Sastri renders tapas as 'devotion' (through concentration); our 'disciplined reflection' fits Shankara's gloss. 'Tapo brahma' = tapas is Brahman, said figuratively (Shankara: by courtesy, as the means).
context: Bhrigu has concluded that food is Brahman, but sees food-born beings come and go and returns to his father. Varuna does not correct him directly; he repeats: seek Brahman through tapas, tapas is Brahman. This repeats after each answer (breath, mind, understanding) until Bhrigu realises that bliss is Brahman.

key_terms.sense: seek to know Brahman through tapas
tapas is Brahman (the means named as the goal)

core_teaching: Real understanding comes through sustained, concentrated inquiry; the teacher keeps sending the student back until the student sees for himself.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: Repeating 'tapas' shows it is the best means: as long as the definition is not fully met and the thirst for more light remains, practise concentration. Varuna calls tapas Brahman by courtesy, because it is the closest means.

commentaries.who: Sureshvara's Vartika (Advaita), notes marked (S.) in A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: By repeatedly saying 'seek Brahman by tapas', the text shows that perception of the self is possible only through such concentrated devotion.

practical_reading: Teachers use it for perseverance in learning and self-inquiry: partial answers are steps, so keep going deeper. Good teachers don't hand over answers too quickly.
misreadings: Tapas here is concentrated reflection, not self-torture
Not a refusal to help
cautions: Low risk.
not_for: someone exhausted who needs rest, not more effort

verified_ref: Taittiriya Upanishad 3.7.1 (Bhriguvalli, anuvaka 7; paras 1-2 in Mahadeva Sastri).
attribution_note: No named speaker after Bhrigu's discovery; 'Teacher -> Reader' is fine.
translation_note: Accurate, though our translation adds 'and breath rests in the body' (śarīre prāṇaḥ pratiṣṭhitaḥ), which is the next clause and not in our Sanskrit. Either extend the Sanskrit or trim the translation.
context: After Bhrigu realises that bliss is Brahman (3.6), the text draws out vows and contemplations. Anuvakas 7-10 pair a vow with a contemplation of food: do not belittle food, do not reject food, make plenty of food, turn no one away. Here, breath and body are food and eater to each other.

key_terms.sense: do not speak ill of food
the body is the eater of food

core_teaching: Because food was the first doorway to knowing Brahman, it should be honoured, never despised; life and body sustain each other as food and eater.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: Since Brahman was known through food, regard food as a teacher and never condemn it; the vow praises food as a means of knowing Brahman. Breath and body rest in each other, so each is both food and eater.

commentaries.who: Sureshvara and Sayana, per Mahadeva Sastri's note (1903)
commentaries.gist: They differ from Shankara: the vow belongs to the contemplation of food as Brahman, so the devotee should never belittle food, treating it as a guru; breaking the vow makes the contemplation defective.

practical_reading: Teachers use it for gratitude and respect toward food: don't complain about or waste it. A footnote in the edition adds that a renunciant should not condemn even poor food that comes by chance.
misreadings: Not a rule against dietary choices or fasting
Not about forcing oneself to eat
cautions: Be careful with readers who have eating disorders; avoid framing around eating amounts.
not_for: someone with an eating disorder
someone experiencing food insecurity, if framed as 'don't complain'

verified_ref: Taittiriya Upanishad 3.10.1 (Bhriguvalli, anuvaka 10; paras 1-3 in Mahadeva Sastri).
translation_note: Translation is accurate, but our Sanskrit field is corrupted: it begins with two stray headings, 'सदाचारप्रदर्शनम् । ब्रह्मानन्दानुभवः', that are not part of the verse, and is missing a space before 'न कञ्चन'. The verse proper is 'न कंचन वसतौ प्रत्याचक्षीत । तद्व्रतम् । तस्माद्यया कया च विधया बह्वन्नं प्राप्नुयात् । अराध्यस्मा अन्नमित्याचक्षते ॥'. 'Yayā kayā ca vidhayā' = by whatever means; Shankara and Sayana assume lawful means (Sayana lists officiating, teaching, accepting gifts).
context: The last of the food vows in the Bhriguvalli, following the contemplation of earth and space as food and eater. Whoever practises it must never refuse lodging to anyone who comes, and so must earn plenty of food to feed guests; the wise say 'food is ready for him'. The section then says food given generously and respectfully comes back the same way.

key_terms.sense: turn no one away (who seeks) lodging
one should obtain plenty of food

core_teaching: Hospitality is a sacred vow: never turn away someone seeking shelter, and so work to have enough to share.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: The one who contemplates earth and space must not turn away anyone seeking lodging; since lodging implies food, he should earn plenty of food by every means. The wise say 'food is ready' rather than send a guest away.

commentaries.who: Sayana's commentary (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: A host who lets a guest go hungry loses all good here and hereafter; earn food by officiating, teaching, accepting gifts. Food given in one's prime and with respect returns the same way, at the same stage of life.

practical_reading: Teachers use it for generosity and open-door hospitality: earn well partly so that you can share. In a modern key, welcome guests, newcomers and people in need.
misreadings: 'By whatever means' is not a licence for dishonest earning; the commentators assume proper means
Not a demand to put oneself or family at risk by admitting anyone
cautions: Someone financially struggling may feel guilty; frame as sharing what one can.
Personal safety comes first.
speaks_to: work as a means to share
not_for: someone in financial hardship
someone who cannot safely open their home
